title: Apache HTTP Server / httpd
analogy: Think of httpd as a hotel front desk: every arriving guest (HTTP request) is greeted, checked against the hotel's rules (virtual host/directory configuration, access control), and either handed a room key directly (static file served) or directed to the right department (reverse-proxied to a backend application) — with the front desk staffing model (MPM: one dedicated clerk per guest vs. a pool of clerks handling many guests concurrently) determined by which MPM is active.

sections.code:
Client
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP 80 / 443
   ↓
httpd listening socket
   ↓
VirtualHost matching (by hostname/port)
   ↓
Directory/Location access control + modules (mod_ssl, mod_proxy, etc.)
   ↓
Permissions / SELinux (httpd_t, httpd_sys_content_t for served files)
   ↓
Static file served, OR reverse-proxied to backend application
   ↓
Response → Client

rpm -q httpd                       # 🟢
sudo dnf install httpd mod_ssl     # 🟡 mod_ssl needed for TLS support
httpd -V                            # 🟢 version, compiled-in MPM, config file paths compiled in

p: Always validate config before reload/restart:
sections.code:
systemctl status httpd
systemctl start httpd
systemctl stop httpd            # 🔴 removes web service availability immediately
systemctl restart httpd         # 🟠 drops all current connections; brief full outage during restart
systemctl reload httpd          # 🟡 gracefully re-reads configuration, allowing in-flight requests to complete — strongly preferred over restart for config changes
systemctl enable httpd
systemctl disable httpd         # 🔴 do not disable on a production web server without a compensating plan
systemctl is-active httpd
systemctl is-enabled httpd

sudo httpd -t          # 🟢 "Syntax OK" or a specific error with file/line

list: Main config: `/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`
Module loading: `/etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/*.conf`
Additional/vhost config: `/etc/httpd/conf.d/*.conf` (site-specific and module-specific configuration typically lives here, included automatically)
Default document root: `/var/www/html/`
Logs: `/var/log/httpd/access_log`, `/var/log/httpd/error_log` (plus per-vhost logs if configured).
TLS certs/keys (with mod_ssl): typically `/etc/pki/tls/certs/`, `/etc/pki/tls/private/`.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`Listen` — Which port(s)/addresses to bind — `Listen 8080` — Adds/changes the listening port — requires matching firewalld AND SELinux port label changes if non-standard

`DocumentRoot` — Where static content is served from — `DocumentRoot "/var/www/html"` — Determines the base directory for a (virtual) host's content — must be labeled `httpd_sys_content_t` for SELinux to permit serving
`<VirtualHost *:443>` block — Per-site/per-port configuration — includes `ServerName`, `SSLCertificateFile`, etc. — Enables hosting multiple distinct sites/certs on one httpd instance
`ProxyPass` / `ProxyPassReverse` (mod_proxy) — Reverse-proxy configuration — `ProxyPass "/api" "http://127.0.0.1:8081/"` — Forwards matching requests to a backend application server
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
TCP — 80 — HTTP (unencrypted) — Commonly kept open only to redirect to HTTPS
TCP — 443 — HTTPS (TLS) — Primary production listener; requires `mod_ssl`, valid certificates, and modern TLS configuration (disable outdated protocol versions/ciphers per current guidance)
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep httpd     # 🟢 confirm listening ports

list: Service dependencies: systemd; commonly fronts a separate application backend (PHP-FPM, a Node/Python app server, etc.) via `mod_proxy`.
Network dependencies: firewalld allowing 80/443; DNS for virtual host resolution from clients.
Storage dependencies: document root and log directories must exist with correct ownership/permissions.
Authentication dependencies: optional — Basic/Digest auth via `.htaccess`/`<Directory>` blocks, or delegated to an upstream identity provider for proxied applications.

Security dependencies: SELinux `httpd_t` and its numerous booleans (`httpd_can_network_connect`, `httpd_can_network_connect_db`, etc.) frequently need explicit enabling for non-trivial deployments (e.g., proxying, database connections) — see Section 11.
Configuration dependencies: `httpd -t` syntax validity before every reload/restart; correct SELinux content labeling for any nonstandard document root.

p: Objective: Add a new virtual host serving from a nonstandard document root.
Verification:
Expected result: the new site is served; confirm firewalld already permits 80/443 (usually already open if httpd was previously in use) and SELinux content labeling is correct.
Objective: Enable a commonly needed boolean for a reverse-proxy configuration.
sections.code:
sudo mkdir -p /srv/mysite/public_html # 🟡 echo "

hello

" | sudo tee /srv/mysite/public_html/index.html sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mysite/public_html(/.*)?" # 🟡 (Profile 5) sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/mysite/public_html # 🟡 sudo tee /etc/httpd/conf.d/mysite.conf <<'EOF' ServerName mysite.example.com DocumentRoot /srv/mysite/public_html EOF sudo httpd -t # 🟢 validate BEFORE reload sudo systemctl reload httpd # 🟡 curl -H "Host: mysite.example.com" http://localhost/ # 🟢 local test # then test from a REMOTE host, not just localhost sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on # 🟡 (Profile 5) — required for httpd to make outbound connections to a proxied backend

list: Authentication/Authorization: per-`<Directory>`/`.htaccess` access control; delegate to the backend application for anything beyond simple cases.
Privilege requirements: httpd's master process starts as root (to bind privileged ports 80/443) but worker processes run as an unprivileged user (`apache` by convention).
Least privilege: keep the document root's ownership/permissions minimal (readable by `apache`, not writable unless the application specifically requires it).

Network exposure: internet-facing httpd should terminate TLS with a modern configuration (`mod_ssl` with current protocol/cipher guidance — consult current Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator or Red Hat crypto-policy guidance rather than hardcoding a specific cipher list here, since recommended defaults evolve).
Firewall requirements: open only 80/443 (or your actual listening ports) — not broader ranges.
Sensitive files: TLS private keys (`/etc/pki/tls/private/`) must be root-readable only.
Logging/Auditing: `access_log`/`error_log` should feed into centralized logging (Profile 10/SIEM) for security monitoring.
Required security configuration: current TLS protocol/cipher baseline; correct SELinux content labeling; least-privilege document root permissions.
Optional hardening: `mod_security` (WAF) for additional application-layer protection, HSTS headers, restrictive `<Directory>` defaults (deny-by-default, allow specific paths).

p: This is one of the most common SELinux+service pairings administrators encounter: a functioning app that suddenly can't reach a database or backend after being moved to RHEL, almost always resolved with the correct boolean rather than disabling enforcement.
sections.code:

ps -Z | grep httpd                          # expect httpd_t
ls -Z /var/www/html/                        # expect httpd_sys_content_t
getsebool -a | grep httpd                   # list all httpd-related booleans
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on   # needed for outbound proxy/backend connections
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on   # needed if httpd/a PHP app connects directly to a remote database

ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c httpd

firewall-cmd --list-services | grep -E 'http|https'

firewall-cmd --reload    # 🟠

journalctl -u httpd                       # 🟢 daemon lifecycle events
tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log          # 🟢 application-level errors (config, module, per-request 500s)
tail -f /var/log/httpd/access_log         # 🟢 per-request access log

systemctl is-active httpd
httpd -t
ss -lntup | grep httpd
firewall-cmd --list-services
getenforce
curl -I http://localhost/       # confirm a response locally
curl -I http://SERVER_IP/       # confirm from a REMOTE host

list: Availability: always `reload` (not `restart`) for config changes where possible; validate with `httpd -t` first, every time.

Performance: choose MPM deliberately based on workload (`event`/`worker` for high-concurrency, I/O-bound; `prefork` if a non-thread-safe module like classic `mod_php` requires it — verify your actual compiled default per the note in Section 1).
Security: keep TLS configuration current; disable `.htaccess` where not needed (`AllowOverride None`) for both performance and reduced attack surface.
Monitoring: monitor `access_log`/`error_log` volume and error rates; monitor certificate expiry proactively.
Configuration management: manage vhost configs via configuration management for fleet consistency; validate with `httpd -t` as a pre-deploy gate.
Disaster recovery: back up TLS private keys/certs securely and separately from general config backups.

p: High latency or connection exhaustion is often an MPM tuning issue (`MaxRequestWorkers` and related directives too low for the actual concurrency) or a slow backend the reverse proxy is waiting on — distinguish the two before tuning httpd itself.
sections.code:
top / ps aux | grep httpd        # 🟢 worker process count/resource usage
ss -s                             # 🟢 connection state summary
tail -f /var/log/httpd/access_log | awk '{print $NF}'   # 🟢 quick look at response codes/sizes for anomalies (adapt to your actual log format)
apachectl status  (if mod_status enabled)                # 🟢 detailed live worker/connection status

lab.text: Confirm httpd installed/active; `httpd -t`.
Serve a simple static page from the default document root; verify with `curl`.
Create a new vhost on a nonstandard document root; apply correct SELinux labeling; verify.
Enable `mod_ssl` and configure a self-signed cert for lab TLS testing.
Configure a simple `ProxyPass` to a second lab service; enable `httpd_can_network_connect`; verify end-to-end.
(Lab VM only) Introduce a deliberate syntax error; run `httpd -t` and observe the specific error reported.
(Lab VM only) Remove the SELinux boolean/content label for the proxy example and observe the resulting failure; troubleshoot with `ausearch`.
Fix and re-verify from a second lab VM (not just `curl localhost`).

failures.fix: 🔴 Editing `httpd.conf`/vhost files and `restart`ing (dropping all live connections) instead of `reload`ing after validating with `httpd -t`.
🟡 Forgetting SELinux content labeling (`httpd_sys_content_t`) on a nonstandard document root — classic "403 Forbidden despite correct Unix permissions."
🟡 Forgetting `httpd_can_network_connect`/`_db` booleans when introducing a reverse proxy or direct database connection.
🟡 Changing `Listen` port without updating both firewalld and the SELinux port label.
🟡 Testing only via `curl localhost` and declaring success without a remote-host test.
🟠 Leaving outdated TLS protocol versions/ciphers enabled long after they're no longer recommended.

trouble: Problem: Site returns 403/500, or is unreachable.

title: auditd
analogy: Think of auditd as a courthouse stenographer assigned specifically to record a predefined list of "notable events" (not everything that happens, everything would be unusable) — every time someone touches a watched file, runs a watched syscall, or SELinux blocks something, the stenographer writes an exact, timestamped, attributable record that can later be read back verbatim in court (an investigation/audit).

sections.code:
Kernel syscall / file access / SELinux AVC event
   ↓
Kernel audit framework (filters against loaded rules)
   ↓
auditd (userspace daemon) receives matching events
   ↓
/var/log/audit/audit.log (structured, append-only)
   ↓
ausearch / aureport (query tools) ── and/or ── audisp plugins (forward to SIEM/remote syslog)

rpm -q audit                      # 🟢 present by default on RHEL 7+
sudo dnf install audit            # 🟡 rarely needed
auditctl -s                       # 🟢 shows kernel audit subsystem status

p: Critical exception to normal systemd practice: Red Hat's own guidance explicitly advises against `systemctl restart auditd` — restarting can lose audit events during the gap and, in some configurations, auditd is intentionally difficult to stop (it can be configured to be effectively un-disable-able at runtime for compliance reasons, requiring a reboot with an altered kernel parameter to fully disable). Use instead:
Always verify current guidance with `man auditd` on your system, since this is an area where auditd deliberately diverges from standard systemd unit conventions covered in Profile 1.
sections.code:
systemctl status auditd
systemctl start auditd
systemctl enable auditd
systemctl is-active auditd
systemctl is-enabled auditd

sudo service auditd reload         # 🟡 (yes, the older `service` wrapper — this is the Red-Hat-documented supported path for auditd specifically, not systemctl)
sudo auditctl -e 1                 # 🟡 alternative: signal enable/reload via auditctl itself

list: Daemon config: `/etc/audit/auditd.conf` — log rotation, space-management behavior, log format.
Rules (persistent, loaded at boot): `/etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules` (compiled by `augenrules` into `/etc/audit/audit.rules` at boot/service start).
Runtime rules (session-only, lost on restart unless also in rules.d): managed live via `auditctl -a ...`.
Log file: `/var/log/audit/audit.log`.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`max_log_file` (auditd.conf) — Max size of a single log file before rotation — `max_log_file = 50` (MB) — Controls rotation granularity
`max_log_file_action` — What to do when the size limit is hit — `max_log_file_action = rotate` — Rotates rather than stopping logging

`space_left_action` / `admin_space_left_action` — What to do as disk space runs low — `space_left_action = email` then eventually `admin_space_left_action = halt` (STIG-driven configurations sometimes mandate halting the system rather than silently losing audit coverage) — Determines whether the system prioritizes availability or guaranteed audit-trail completeness under disk pressure — a deliberate, consequential choice, not a default to change casually

`-w PATH -p PERMS -k KEYNAME` (rule syntax) — Watch a file/directory for given access types, tagged with a searchable key — `-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes` — Every write/attribute-change to `/etc/passwd` is logged and searchable via `ausearch -k passwd_changes`

p: auditd itself has no network listener. Remote log shipping (if configured via `audisp-remote`/syslog forwarding) uses whatever protocol/port that specific plugin/destination requires — treat as a distinct network dependency, not auditd's own.

list: Service dependencies: kernel audit framework (built into the kernel, not a separate service); systemd for lifecycle management (with the caveats in Section 5).
Network dependencies: none for local-only auditing; relevant only if remote forwarding is configured.
Storage dependencies: `/var/log/audit/` must have adequate space — `space_left_action`/`admin_space_left_action` govern behavior as it fills.
Authentication dependencies: none directly; auditd records authentication events from PAM/sshd/etc.
Security dependencies: SELinux confines `auditd_t`; SELinux AVC denials themselves flow through this same subsystem, making auditd foundational to Profile 5's own troubleshooting.
Configuration dependencies: rule syntax correctness (`augenrules --check` / `auditctl -l` to verify loaded rules match intent); file permissions on `auditd.conf` (STIG guidance specifies `0640`).

p: Objective: Add a persistent watch rule for changes to `/etc/passwd`.
Verification:
Expected result: any future write/attribute change to `/etc/passwd` is logged and searchable by the `passwd_changes` key.
Objective: Search for all failed login attempts today.
sections.code:
sudo tee /etc/audit/rules.d/50-passwd-watch.rules <<'EOF'
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes
EOF
sudo augenrules --load                  # 🟡 compiles rules.d into the active ruleset and loads them without a restart

sudo auditctl -l | grep passwd          # 🟢 confirm rule is loaded
sudo touch /etc/passwd                  # 🟡 (or make a real change) to generate a test event — touch alone updates the timestamp/attribute, matching -p a
ausearch -k passwd_changes -ts recent   # 🟢 confirm the event was captured

ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -su no -ts today    # 🟢 (exact message-type/filter syntax varies by audit version — verify with `ausearch --help` and `man ausearch` on your system)
aureport --auth -i                          # 🟢 summarized, interpreted authentication report

list: Authentication/Authorization: modifying audit rules requires root; the audit subsystem itself can optionally be configured (via `-e 2` "lock" rule) to make its configuration immutable until reboot, a common compliance requirement preventing an attacker (or an over-eager administrator) from silently disabling auditing mid-session.
Least privilege: restrict read access to `/var/log/audit/audit.log` (root-only by default, `0600`) — it can contain sensitive operational detail.
Privilege requirements: all rule changes and config edits require root.
Sensitive files: `/etc/audit/auditd.conf` (STIG-recommended `0640`), `/var/log/audit/audit.log` (`0600`), rule files under `/etc/audit/rules.d/`.

Logging/Auditing: this is the auditing layer — ensure `space_left_action`/`admin_space_left_action` reflect your organization's actual tolerance for potentially losing audit coverage vs. system availability under disk pressure.

Required security configuration: a syscall-auditing baseline appropriate to your compliance framework (many organizations start from a published STIG/CIS rule set rather than authoring one from scratch); correct file permissions per Section above.
Optional hardening: the `-e 2` immutable-configuration lock (requires a reboot to change rules afterward — a deliberate trade-off between flexibility and tamper-resistance).
Never disable auditd as a way to "reduce noise" on a compliance-scoped system — tune rules instead of removing the entire audit trail.

p: auditd and SELinux have a uniquely tight relationship: every SELinux denial is an audit event, so a healthy, running auditd is a prerequisite for effective SELinux troubleshooting throughout this handbook, not merely a peer concern.
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep auditd            # expect auditd_t
ls -Z /var/log/audit/
ausearch -m avc -ts recent     # auditd is literally the mechanism that surfaces AVC denials — see Profile 5

p: Not applicable to local-only auditd operation. If remote audit-event forwarding is configured (e.g., via `audisp-remote` to a central collector), treat the destination port/protocol like any other network dependency requiring appropriate outbound allowance and, on the receiving collector, standard inbound firewalld/SELinux configuration.
auditd is a logging system, but it has its own meta-logging (daemon health) separate from the audit records themselves:

Correlate `ausearch -m avc` (SELinux denials, Profile 5) with `ausearch -m USER_AUTH`/`USER_LOGIN` (authentication events) and application-specific logs (`journalctl -u SERVICE`) for a complete incident timeline.
sections.code:
journalctl -u auditd                       # 🟢 daemon lifecycle events (start/stop/reload), not the audit records themselves
ausearch -ts recent                        # 🟢 the actual audit records
aureport --summary                         # 🟢 high-level summarized report across all recorded categories
aureport --failed -i                       # 🟢 failed events specifically, interpreted (-i) into readable names

systemctl is-active auditd
auditctl -s                     # confirm "enabled" and check "lost" event counter (should be 0 or stable, not climbing)
auditctl -l                     # confirm expected rules are loaded
ls -la /var/log/audit/audit.log # confirm actively growing, correct permissions (0600)

list: Availability: carefully choose `space_left_action`/`admin_space_left_action` — understand that maximizing audit-trail completeness (`halt`) trades directly against system availability.
Reliability: monitor the `lost` event counter (`auditctl -s`) as a first-class metric.
Performance: avoid unnecessarily broad syscall rules on high-throughput systems; scope watches to genuinely sensitive paths/syscalls.
Configuration management: manage `/etc/audit/rules.d/` centrally so the rule baseline is consistent and auditable across the fleet.
Disaster recovery/compliance: forward audit events to a remote, access-controlled log collector for tamper-resistant retention if regulatory requirements demand it.

p: Excessive syscall-rule scope on a busy system is the most common auditd-related performance concern — narrow the rule set to genuinely required paths/syscalls rather than tuning the daemon itself.
sections.code:
auditctl -s                     # 🟢 backlog/lost-event counters — a leading indicator of overload
top / ps                        # 🟢 confirm auditd's own CPU/memory footprint isn't unexpectedly high
iostat -x 1                     # 🟢 disk I/O if very broad rules are generating heavy log-write volume

lab.text: Confirm auditd installed/active: `systemctl is-active auditd`, `auditctl -s`.
Add a persistent watch rule for a lab file; load with `augenrules --load`.
Trigger the watched action; confirm capture with `ausearch -k`.
Review `aureport --summary` output.

(Lab VM only) Deliberately misconfigure `admin_space_left_action = halt` with a small dedicated audit log partition and fill it, observing the resulting behavior — never attempt this outside an isolated lab VM.
Troubleshoot using the Section 15 chain (space, lost counter).
Recover by freeing space / adjusting configuration, verify normal logging resumes.
Practice the documented `service auditd reload` path instead of `systemctl restart`.

failures.fix: 🔴 Running `systemctl restart auditd` reflexively (as one would for any other daemon) instead of the documented `service auditd reload`/`auditctl` path — risks losing events or hitting version-specific restart restrictions.
🟡 Adding a rule via `auditctl` only (runtime) and forgetting to also persist it under `/etc/audit/rules.d/` — the rule vanishes on next boot/reload.

🟡 Writing overly broad watch rules (e.g., watching an entire busy directory tree at the syscall level) that generate excessive log volume, risking rotation/space pressure that then drops genuinely important events.

🟠 Setting `admin_space_left_action = halt` without understanding the operational consequence — a full audit partition will halt the system by design in that configuration, a deliberate compliance choice that must be a conscious decision, not a default left unexamined.
🟡 Ignoring the `lost` event counter in `auditctl -s` — a climbing value means events are being dropped, silently undermining the audit trail's completeness.
🟡 Assuming journald alone (Profile 6) is an adequate substitute for compliance-grade auditing — it lacks the syscall-level granularity and rule-driven precision auditd provides.

trouble: Problem: Expected events aren't appearing in the audit log.

Service:        auditd (Linux Audit daemon)
Package:        audit
systemd unit:   auditd.service
Daemon:         /sbin/auditd
Configuration:  /etc/audit/auditd.conf, /etc/audit/rules.d/
Logs:           /var/log/audit/audit.log
Ports:          none (local only; remote forwarding is a separate plugin/config)

Essential commands:
  auditctl -l
  auditctl -s
  ausearch -k KEYNAME -ts recent
  aureport --summary

Verification:
  auditctl -s shows enabled, lost counter stable

Troubleshooting:
  auditctl -l → augenrules --load → auditctl -s (lost counter, space) → ausearch test

  🔴 Do not `systemctl restart auditd` — use `service auditd reload` per Red Hat guidance.

title: autofs
analogy: Think of autofs as a motion-activated door: the door (mount point) doesn't just sit open (statically mounted) all the time — it stays closed until someone actually walks toward it (a process accesses the path), at which point it opens automatically (mounts on demand), and after nobody's walked through it for a while, it closes itself again (unmounts due to inactivity).

sections.code:
Process accesses a path under an autofs-managed mount point (e.g., /home/someuser)
   ↓
Kernel autofs module intercepts the access, notifies automount daemon
   ↓
automount consults /etc/auto.master and the relevant map (direct or indirect)
   ↓
Determines the actual remote source (e.g., an NFS export) to mount
   ↓
Performs the real mount (commonly NFS, Profile 12) — access now proceeds transparently
   ↓
After a configured idle timeout with no access → automatic unmount

rpm -q autofs                # 🟢
sudo dnf install autofs      # 🟡
automount -V                  # 🟢 version

systemctl status autofs
systemctl start autofs
systemctl stop autofs            # 🟠 currently-mounted autofs-managed mounts may be unmounted; new on-demand mounts won't trigger
systemctl restart autofs         # 🟠 re-reads all maps; existing active mounts are typically preserved across a restart but behavior can vary — verify in your environment
systemctl reload autofs          # 🟡 re-reads /etc/auto.master and map files without unmounting currently active mounts — preferred for map changes
systemctl enable autofs
systemctl is-active autofs

list: Master map: `/etc/auto.master` (or `/etc/auto.master.d/*.autofs`) — defines which mount points autofs manages and which map file governs each.
Map files: e.g., `/etc/auto.home`, `/etc/auto.misc` — define what actually gets mounted for a given key (username, hostname, etc.).
Logs: journald under `autofs` unit.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`/etc/auto.master` entry — Associates a mount-point prefix with a map — `/home /etc/auto.home` — Anything accessed under `/home/*` is resolved via `/etc/auto.home`

Indirect map entry (in `/etc/auto.home`) — Defines the actual source for a given key — `someuser -rw,soft nfs-server:/export/home/someuser` — When `/home/someuser` is accessed, autofs mounts that NFS export there on demand
`--timeout` (master map option) — Idle-unmount timeout in seconds — `/home /etc/auto.home --timeout=300` — Unmounts after 300 seconds of inactivity

p: Not applicable to autofs itself — the protocols in play are whatever the underlying mounted filesystem uses (commonly NFS, Profile 12's ports 2049/111 etc.).

list: Service dependencies: systemd; the kernel `autofs` filesystem module (built-in or loadable).

Network dependencies: whatever the underlying remote filesystem requires (NFS server reachability, firewalld allowance — see Profile 12) — autofs itself adds no new network protocol, it just triggers NFS's existing requirements on demand.
Storage dependencies: none beyond the mount points themselves existing as directories.
Authentication dependencies: commonly paired with SSSD (Profile 14) to resolve per-user home-directory paths dynamically in centralized-identity environments.
Security dependencies: same SELinux/NFS security considerations as Profile 12 apply to whatever autofs actually mounts.
Configuration dependencies: correct map syntax; correct `/etc/auto.master` prefix-to-map association.

p: Objective: Configure on-demand NFS home directory mounting.
(The `*` wildcard key with `&` substitution is a common indirect-map pattern: it matches any username and substitutes it into the NFS path, avoiding a separate map line per user.)
Verification:
Expected result: the NFS home directory mounts transparently on first access and unmounts automatically after the idle period.
sections.code:
sudo tee -a /etc/auto.master.d/home.autofs <<'EOF'
/home /etc/auto.home --timeout=600
EOF
sudo tee /etc/auto.home <<'EOF'
*    -rw,soft,intr    nfs-server:/export/home/&
EOF
sudo systemctl reload autofs    # 🟡

ls /home/someuser              # 🟢 the access itself triggers the mount
mount | grep someuser          # 🟢 confirm it's now actually mounted
# wait past the configured timeout with no further access, then:
mount | grep someuser          # 🟢 confirm it auto-unmounted

list: Authentication/Authorization: autofs itself adds no new authentication layer — whatever the underlying mounted filesystem's security model is (e.g., NFS's `AUTH_SYS`/Kerberos options, Profile 12) applies unchanged.

Optional hardening: short idle timeouts reduce the window during which a given mount remains active/exposed after last use.

title: BIND / named
analogy: Think of named as a very well-organized reference librarian: for zones the library owns (authoritative), it gives out its own definitive answer immediately. For everything else (recursive mode), it goes and asks other libraries (other DNS servers) on your behalf, remembers (caches) the answer for a while so it doesn't have to ask again, and hands you the result.

sections.code:
Client (or another resolver)
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP/UDP 53
   ↓
named
   ↓
named.conf (options, zone declarations, access control lists)
   ↓
   ├── Authoritative: zone files (/var/named/) — served directly
   └── Recursive: queries upstream/root servers, caches results per TTL
   ↓
Permissions / SELinux (named_t, named_zone_t for zone files)
   ↓
DNS response

rpm -q bind bind-utils              # 🟢
sudo dnf install bind bind-utils    # 🟡
named -v                             # 🟢 version
named-checkconf                      # 🟢 validates named.conf syntax (run with no args after install to sanity-check the default config)

p: Preferred administrative control channel — `rndc` (avoids a full systemd-level restart for many operations):
sections.code:
systemctl status named
systemctl start named
systemctl stop named            # 🔴 all DNS resolution/authority this server provides stops immediately
systemctl restart named         # 🟠 brief outage during restart; in-flight queries fail and must be retried by clients
systemctl reload named          # 🟡 re-reads zone files/config without dropping the listening socket — preferred for zone updates; equivalent to `rndc reload`
systemctl enable named
systemctl is-active named

sudo rndc reload                    # 🟡 reload all zones/config, equivalent to systemctl reload
sudo rndc reload ZONE               # 🟡 reload just one zone, minimizing scope of the change
sudo rndc status                    # 🟢 detailed operational status

list: Main config: `/etc/named.conf`
Zone files: `/var/named/` (e.g., `/var/named/example.com.zone`)
rndc key/config: `/etc/rndc.key`, referenced from `named.conf`
Logs: journald under `named` unit; can also be configured to log to specific files via `named.conf`'s `logging` block.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`zone "example.com" { type master; file "example.com.zone"; };` — Declares an authoritative zone — (as shown) — This server becomes authoritative for `example.com`, serving from the named zone file

`allow-recursion { ... };` — Which clients may use this server for recursive lookups — `allow-recursion { 192.168.0.0/24; };` — Critical security setting — an open recursive resolver reachable from the internet is a well-known abuse vector (DNS amplification attacks); always restrict this to trusted networks

`also-notify` / `allow-transfer` — Zone transfer (replication) control — `allow-transfer { 192.168.1.5; };` — Restricts which secondary servers may pull full zone data — leaving this open exposes your entire zone data to anyone who asks

Serial number (in the zone file's SOA record) — Zone version tracking — incrementing integer — Must be incremented on every zone file change or secondary servers won't detect the update — a very common operational mistake
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
UDP — 53 — Standard DNS queries — Primary DNS protocol port
TCP — 53 — Zone transfers, large/truncated responses, DNS-over-TCP fallback — Required for zone transfers (`allow-transfer`) between primary/secondary servers
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep named    # 🟢 confirm listening

list: Service dependencies: systemd; SELinux `named_t`/`named_zone_t` policy.
Network dependencies: firewalld allowing UDP/TCP 53; for recursive mode, outbound connectivity to the wider DNS hierarchy (root/TLD servers or configured forwarders).
Storage dependencies: `/var/named/` for zone files, with correct ownership (`named` user/group) and SELinux labeling.
Authentication dependencies: `rndc` uses a shared key for administrative control channel authentication; zone transfers can use TSIG keys for authenticated, integrity-protected transfers.
Security dependencies: correctly restricted `allow-recursion`/`allow-transfer`; DNSSEC configuration if zone integrity validation is required.
Configuration dependencies: `named-checkconf` and `named-checkzone` validation before every reload; correct SOA serial incrementing on zone changes.

p: Objective: Add a new authoritative zone.
Verification:
Expected result: the new zone resolves correctly; test from a remote client on the intended network to confirm reachability, not just localhost.
Objective: Increment a zone's serial after editing a record (required every time).
sections.code:
sudo tee -a /etc/named.conf <<'EOF'
zone "example.internal" {
    type master;
    file "example.internal.zone";
    allow-transfer { 192.168.1.5; };
};
EOF
sudo tee /var/named/example.internal.zone <<'EOF'
$TTL 3600
@   IN SOA ns1.example.internal. admin.example.internal. (
        2026092201 ; serial
        3600       ; refresh
        900        ; retry
        604800     ; expire
        3600 )     ; minimum
    IN NS  ns1.example.internal.
ns1 IN A   192.168.1.10
www IN A   192.168.1.20
EOF
sudo chown root:named /var/named/example.internal.zone            # 🟡
sudo chmod 640 /var/named/example.internal.zone                    # 🟡
sudo named-checkconf                                                # 🟢 validate config
sudo named-checkzone example.internal /var/named/example.internal.zone   # 🟢 validate zone file
sudo systemctl reload named                                         # 🟡 (or `rndc reload`)

dig @localhost example.internal            # 🟢 query the server directly
dig @localhost www.example.internal        # 🟢

# edit the zone file, bump the serial number
sudo named-checkzone example.internal /var/named/example.internal.zone   # 🟢
sudo rndc reload example.internal          # 🟡 reload just this zone

list: Authentication/Authorization: `rndc` shared-key authentication for administrative control; TSIG keys for authenticated zone transfers.

Network exposure: an open recursive resolver (answering recursive queries from any source on the internet) is a serious, well-known abuse vector for DNS amplification DDoS attacks — this is one of the highest-priority security settings in this entire handbook to get right.
Firewall requirements: restrict UDP/TCP 53 to only the networks that should query this server; restrict recursion (`allow-recursion`) independently of network-layer firewall rules, since both matter.
Sensitive files: `/etc/rndc.key` and any TSIG keys.

Required security configuration: `allow-recursion` scoped to trusted networks only (never open to the internet unless you specifically intend to operate a public recursive resolver with appropriate rate-limiting/abuse mitigation); `allow-transfer` scoped to known secondary servers only.

Optional hardening: DNSSEC signing for authoritative zones; `bind-chroot` for additional process isolation (verify current availability/guidance for your RHEL 10 point release); response rate limiting (RRL) to mitigate abuse even for legitimately-scoped recursive service.

p: A common SELinux issue: a zone file created/copied without correct labeling causes `named` to fail loading that zone — `restorecon -Rv /var/named/` resolves typical cases.

ps -Z | grep named                    # expect named_t
ls -Z /var/named/                     # expect named_zone_t (or similar) on zone files

p: Scope this to the appropriate zone/source restrictions if the server should only answer specific networks — firewalld's `--add-service=dns` alone doesn't restrict which clients may query, only that the port is open; combine with `allow-recursion`/`allow-query` in `named.conf` for the actual access-control layer, and consider firewalld rich rules restricting source subnets for defense in depth.

list: Availability: run redundant (primary + secondary) authoritative servers for any zone you're authoritative for; use `rndc reload ZONE` for minimal-scope updates rather than reloading everything.
Security: restrict `allow-recursion`/`allow-transfer` tightly; consider DNSSEC for zone integrity; consider response rate limiting even for legitimately-scoped recursive service.
Monitoring: monitor query volume/patterns for anomalies (potential abuse or amplification attempts); monitor zone-transfer success between primary/secondary.

Configuration management: manage zone files and `named.conf` via version control/configuration management, with automated serial-number incrementing where possible to eliminate the manual-mistake risk.
Disaster recovery: back up zone files and `named.conf`; ensure secondary servers provide continuity if the primary is unavailable.

p: A recursive resolver under heavy load or facing abuse (e.g., serving as an unwitting DDoS amplifier due to open recursion) can show high CPU/network usage — correlate unusual query volume/patterns with `allow-recursion` scope as a first check before assuming it's simply organic load growth.

dig +stats @localhost example.com     # 🟢 response time for a specific query

title: chronyd
analogy: Think of chronyd as a diligent clock-checker who doesn't just glance at one reference clock once and trust it — it continuously polls several trusted reference clocks (NTP servers), statistically weighs how reliable each one has been, and gently (not abruptly) nudges your system's clock to converge on the best estimate of true time, adjusting the clock's speed rather than just jumping the time, to avoid breaking anything that depends on time moving forward smoothly.

sections.code:
Upstream NTP source(s) (pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org, or internal stratum server)
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — UDP/123
   ↓
chronyd (client mode: polls sources; server mode: also listens for client requests)
   ↓
chrony.conf (server list, drift file, step/slew policy)
   ↓
Kernel system clock (adjusted via adjtimex, slewed or stepped)
   ↓
Hardware RTC (optionally synced via rtcsync, for correct time across reboots before network is up)

rpm -q chrony                    # 🟢 present by default on nearly all RHEL 10 installs
sudo dnf install chrony          # 🟡 rarely needed
chronyd -v                       # 🟢 version
rpm -q ntp && systemctl is-active ntpd   # 🟢 confirm the legacy, deprecated ntpd is NOT also present/running

systemctl status chronyd
systemctl start chronyd
systemctl stop chronyd            # 🟠 clock will drift uncorrected until restarted
systemctl restart chronyd         # 🟡 brief resync needed after restart, low practical risk for most workloads
systemctl reload chronyd          # chronyd's ExecReload typically re-reads config similarly to restart for most directive changes — verify with `systemctl cat chronyd`; when in doubt use restart for config changes
systemctl enable chronyd
systemctl disable chronyd         # 🟠 do not disable without an alternative time-sync mechanism
systemctl is-active chronyd
systemctl is-enabled chronyd

list: Main config: `/etc/chrony.conf`
Drift file: `/var/lib/chrony/drift` (records the system clock's characteristic drift rate to speed up future convergence — persistent data, not configuration).
Key file (if authenticated NTP is used): `/etc/chrony.keys`
Logs: journald under `chronyd` unit; optional file logging to `/var/log/chrony/` if `logdir`/`log` directives are set.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`pool` / `server` — Upstream time source(s) — `pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst` — `pool` resolves to multiple servers via DNS for redundancy; `iburst` speeds initial sync by sending a burst of requests
`driftfile` — Where to persist clock-drift characteristics — `driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift` — Speeds convergence after restarts/reboots by remembering how fast this particular clock drifts

`makestep` — When/how many times to allow an immediate step vs. gradual slew — `makestep 1.0 3` — Steps the clock if offset exceeds 1.0s, but only for the first 3 updates (typically at startup) — avoids disruptive time jumps later during normal operation

`allow` — Which clients/subnets may query this host as an NTP server — `allow 192.168.0.0/24` — Required if operating chronyd in server mode for a local network; absent by default (client-only posture)
`rtcsync` — Keep the hardware RTC synced via kernel — `rtcsync` — Improves clock accuracy immediately after boot, before network sync completes
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations

UDP — 123 — NTP client/server communication — If operating as a server reachable from untrusted networks, restrict via `allow`/firewalld source rules and consider `ratelimit` to mitigate abuse/amplification concerns
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep chronyd    # 🟢 confirm listening (server mode) or outbound-only (client mode)

list: Service dependencies: systemd; independent of other daemons functionally.
Network dependencies: reachability to configured upstream NTP sources; DNS resolution if using `pool` (hostname-based).
Storage dependencies: `/var/lib/chrony/` for the drift file — must be writable.
Authentication dependencies: optional NTP symmetric-key authentication via `/etc/chrony.keys` for server/client trust in security-sensitive deployments.
Security dependencies: firewalld allowing UDP/123 if operating in server mode; SELinux `chronyd_t` context.

Configuration dependencies: downstream services that depend on accurate time (Kerberos/SSSD, TLS-based services, distributed databases) implicitly depend on chronyd being correctly synced — this is a frequently underappreciated dependency chain.

p: Objective: Confirm current sync status and source quality.
Objective: Configure chronyd as a server for an internal subnet.
Verification:
sections.code:
chronyc tracking     # 🟢 current offset, stratum, reference source
chronyc sources -v   # 🟢 per-source reachability, offset, selection state
timedatectl           # 🟢 higher-level summary including "System clock synchronized: yes/no"

sudo tee -a /etc/chrony.conf <<'EOF'

EOF
sudo systemctl restart chronyd                          # 🟡
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=ntp --permanent         # 🟡
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                              # 🟠

firewall-cmd --list-services | grep ntp   # 🟢

list: Authentication: optional symmetric-key NTP authentication for high-assurance environments; most deployments trust public/internal pools without it, accepting the inherent trust model of NTP.
Authorization: `allow`/`deny` directives control who may query this host as a time server.

Privilege requirements: chronyd runs as its own unprivileged `chrony` user internally (dropping root after binding required resources), per standard hardened-daemon design — verify with `ps -Z`/`ps aux` on your system.
Network exposure: if operating in server mode facing untrusted networks, restrict source ranges and consider rate-limiting to reduce amplification-style abuse risk.
Sensitive files: `/etc/chrony.keys` if authenticated NTP is used.
Required security configuration: don't expose an open (unrestricted `allow 0.0.0.0/0`) NTP server to the public internet without a clear operational reason and rate-limiting.
Optional hardening: symmetric-key authentication between trusted internal server/client pairs.

p: SELinux issues with chronyd are uncommon in stock configurations; most commonly arise if the drift file or an alternate config path is placed somewhere with an unexpected label — `restorecon -Rv /var/lib/chrony/` resolves typical cases.

list: Availability: configure multiple redundant upstream sources (`pool` with `maxsources`, or several explicit `server` lines) so a single unreachable source doesn't leave the host unsynced.
Reliability: in virtualized/cloud environments, explicitly decide whether chronyd or the hypervisor's own time-sync mechanism is authoritative, and disable the other to avoid conflict.
Monitoring: alert on `chronyc tracking` offset exceeding an organizational threshold, and on "clock not synchronized" conditions.
Configuration management: standardize `chrony.conf` (source list, `allow` rules) across the fleet via configuration management.
Disaster recovery: for isolated/air-gapped networks, ensure an internal authoritative time source is defined rather than relying on unreachable public pools.

p: Time sync itself is rarely a performance bottleneck; the concern is correctness (offset), not throughput:
sections.code:

chronyc sourcestats       # 🟢 per-source stability statistics over time

title: cron / crond
analogy: Think of crond as an alarm clock that checks its own list of alarms every single minute, forever — if the current time matches an entry on the list, it fires that entry's associated command, then goes back to waiting for the next minute.

sections.code:
crond (persistent daemon, wakes every minute)
   ↓
Reads: /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/*, per-user crontabs (/var/spool/cron/*)
   ↓
Time-field match? (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week)
   ↓
Fork + exec the job's command, as the crontab's owning user, with PAM session setup
   ↓
Output (if any) → mailed to MAILTO (if configured) or discarded/logged, depending on config
   ↓
journald / /var/log/cron (via rsyslog, Profile 10) records execution

systemctl is-enabled crond

list: System-wide table: `/etc/crontab` (includes a `run-parts`-style mechanism referencing `/etc/cron.hourly/`, `/etc/cron.daily/`, `/etc/cron.weekly/`, `/etc/cron.monthly/` by default via `cron.d`/`anacron` integration).
Drop-in system jobs: `/etc/cron.d/*` (each file follows the same six-field-plus-user syntax as `/etc/crontab`).
Periodic script directories: `/etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly,monthly}/` — drop executable scripts here rather than editing crontabs directly, for simple periodic tasks.
Per-user crontabs: `/var/spool/cron/USERNAME` — never edit directly; always use `crontab -e` (which validates syntax and sets correct permissions).
Access control: `/etc/cron.allow` / `/etc/cron.deny` — restrict which users may use `crontab` at all.
Logs: journald under `crond` unit, traditionally also `/var/log/cron` via rsyslog (Profile 10).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
Five time fields — When to run — `0 2   *` — Minute=0, Hour=2, every day/month/weekday → runs daily at 02:00
`MAILTO=` (in a crontab) — Where to send job output — `MAILTO=admin@example.com` — Job stdout/stderr emailed instead of silently discarded — requires a working local MTA
`@reboot` — Special time spec — `@reboot /path/to/script.sh` — Runs once at crond startup rather than on a recurring schedule

p: Not applicable — cron is not a network service.

list: Service dependencies: systemd; PAM (`/etc/pam.d/crond`) for per-job session setup.
Network dependencies: none for local job execution; individual jobs may of course have their own network dependencies.
Storage dependencies: `/var/spool/cron/` must be writable by the crond process (root) and correctly permissioned per user.
Authentication dependencies: jobs run with the privileges of the crontab's owning user — no additional authentication at execution time.
Security dependencies: SELinux `crond_t` context; `cron.allow`/`cron.deny` for access control.
Configuration dependencies: correct five-field syntax (a common source of "job never ran" bugs); correct `MAILTO`/local mail delivery if relying on email notification of job output.

Least privilege: run each job as the least-privileged user capable of performing it — avoid defaulting to root-owned cron jobs for tasks that don't require it.
Privilege requirements: crond itself runs as root (to be able to execute jobs as any user), but individual jobs execute as their crontab's owner.
Sensitive files: per-user crontabs under `/var/spool/cron/` can reveal operational detail (paths, script names, timing) — protect from unauthorized read.
Network exposure: none directly.

Required security configuration: avoid embedding plaintext credentials directly in crontab command lines (visible via `ps`/`crontab -l` to anyone with appropriate access) — use a credentials file with restricted permissions instead, referenced by the script.
Optional hardening: populate `/etc/cron.allow` explicitly and rely on its allowlist behavior rather than the more permissive default-allow-unless-denied posture.

p: SELinux denials involving cron jobs most often arise when a job's script or target files have unexpected labels (e.g., a script placed somewhere unusual, or writing to a path the job's context isn't permitted to touch) — diagnose with `ausearch`/`restorecon`, not by disabling enforcement.

list: Reliability: implement explicit success/failure alerting for critical jobs (don't rely solely on `MAILTO`) — many organizations wrap cron jobs with a monitoring "dead man's switch"/heartbeat check.
Concurrency: use file-locking (e.g., `flock`) within scripts that must not run concurrently with themselves if a prior invocation might still be running.
Monitoring: track job exit codes and runtime duration over time to catch silent degradation.
Configuration management: manage `/etc/cron.d/` entries via configuration management for fleet consistency and auditability, rather than ad hoc `crontab -e` edits on individual hosts.
Alternative: for complex scheduling needs (dependency chains, richer logging, resource limits), consider systemd timers (`.timer` units, Profile 1) as a more modern alternative to cron on RHEL.

p: crond itself has negligible resource footprint; performance concerns are almost always about the jobs it runs, not crond:
sections.code:

ps aux | grep JOBSCRIPT               # 🟢 check for multiple concurrent instances of a job that should be singular

🟡 Editing `/var/spool/cron/USERNAME` directly instead of via `crontab -e` — bypasses validation and can leave incorrect permissions/ownership.

title: DHCP
analogy: Think of a DHCP server as the front desk at a hotel handing out room keys (IP addresses) to arriving guests (client devices) from a limited pool of available rooms (the address pool/subnet), along with a map of the building (gateway, DNS, other options) — each key is only valid for a set period (the lease time), after which the guest must check back in (renew) or give the room back.

sections.code:
Client (broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER)
   ↓
Network (broadcast domain, or via a relay agent for routed segments)
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — UDP 67 (server) / 68 (client)
   ↓
Kea DHCP server (kea-dhcp4/kea-dhcp6)
   ↓
Kea configuration (JSON) — subnet definitions, pools, options, reservations
   ↓
Lease database (memfile by default, or a configured backend — MySQL/PostgreSQL for larger deployments)
   ↓
DHCPOFFER → DHCPREQUEST → DHCPACK (lease committed)
   ↓
Client applies assigned IP/gateway/DNS/options

rpm -q kea                     # 🟢
sudo dnf install kea           # 🟡
kea-dhcp4 -v                   # 🟢 version — confirm exact invocation/flag on your installed version

systemctl status kea-dhcp4                # verify EXACT unit name on your system first
systemctl start kea-dhcp4
systemctl stop kea-dhcp4            # 🔴 no new leases/renewals served; existing client leases continue until their lease time expires, but renewal will fail
systemctl restart kea-dhcp4         # 🟠 brief service gap; well-behaved clients simply retry
systemctl reload kea-dhcp4          # verify current Kea version's reload support — some Kea versions support live config reload via the control agent/API rather than (or in addition to) a systemd-level reload; consult your version's documentation rather than assuming systemctl reload behaves identically to restart
systemctl enable kea-dhcp4
systemctl is-active kea-dhcp4

p: Migrating from legacy ISC `dhcpd.conf` (RHEL 8/9): ISC provides `keama`, a conversion tool that translates a legacy `dhcpd.conf` into Kea's JSON format as a starting point — review its output carefully rather than trusting it blindly, since not every legacy feature maps cleanly.
list: Main config (JSON format — a significant change from ISC dhcpd's old syntax): typically `/etc/kea/kea-dhcp4.conf` (and `kea-dhcp6.conf` for IPv6) — verify exact path for your installed package layout.

Lease database: default `memfile` backend typically under `/var/lib/kea/` — verify path; larger/HA deployments commonly use a MySQL/PostgreSQL backend instead (see Profile 20 for the database side of that pairing).
Logs: journald under the relevant `kea-*` unit(s); Kea also supports its own structured logging configuration within the JSON config.
Directive (JSON key) — Purpose — Example — Effect
`subnet4` — Defines an IPv4 subnet and its pool — `"subnet": "192.168.1.0/24", "pools": [{"pool": "192.168.1.100 - 192.168.1.200"}]` — Defines the address range Kea may hand out on this subnet
`valid-lifetime` — Lease duration in seconds — `"valid-lifetime": 3600` — How long a client may hold a lease before renewal is required

`reservations` — Static/fixed IP assignment for a specific client (by MAC or other identifier) — `{"hw-address": "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", "ip-address": "192.168.1.50"}` — Guarantees a specific client always receives the same address, functioning similarly to a "DHCP static mapping"
`option-data` — DHCP options to hand out (gateway, DNS, domain, etc.) — `{"name": "routers", "data": "192.168.1.1"}` — Distributes network configuration parameters beyond just the IP address itself
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
UDP — 67 — DHCP server (receives client requests) — Should only be reachable from the intended client subnet(s)/relay agents
UDP — 68 — DHCP client — Client-side; relevant to the requesting device, not the server itself
UDP — 547 — DHCPv6 server (if IPv6 is in use) — Analogous IPv6 considerations
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep kea    # 🟢 confirm listening

list: Service dependencies: systemd; if using a database-backed lease store, the corresponding database service (e.g., Profile 20 PostgreSQL, or MySQL) must be available.
Network dependencies: DHCP relies on broadcast (or a configured relay agent for serving clients on a different subnet than the server itself); firewalld allowing UDP 67 (and 547 for DHCPv6).
Storage dependencies: the lease database location (memfile path, or database connectivity if using a DB backend).
Authentication dependencies: none in the traditional sense — DHCP's trust model is inherently about network access (whoever can broadcast on the segment can request a lease), not credential-based.

Security dependencies: firewalld scoping; network segmentation to prevent rogue DHCP servers on the same broadcast domain (a classic DHCP-related network security concern, mitigated at the switch level via DHCP snooping — outside this RHEL profile's direct control but worth being aware of).
Configuration dependencies: correct subnet/pool definitions that don't overlap with statically assigned addresses elsewhere on the network.

p: Objective: Configure a basic IPv4 subnet with a pool and a static reservation.
Verification:

list: Authentication/Authorization: DHCP has no inherent client authentication — any device on the reachable broadcast domain/relay path can request a lease; this is a structural characteristic of the protocol, not a Kea-specific weakness.
Network exposure: restrict DHCP service reachability to only the intended client subnets, both via firewalld and via actual network segmentation/VLAN design.

Rogue server risk: an unauthorized/rogue DHCP server on the same broadcast domain can hijack client configuration (a classic attack/misconfiguration vector) — mitigated primarily at the network switch level (DHCP snooping) rather than within Kea itself, but administrators should be aware this is a shared responsibility with network infrastructure.
Sensitive files: the Kea configuration reveals network topology (subnets, reservations tied to specific hardware) — protect from unauthorized read/write.
Required security configuration: scope the server to only the interfaces/subnets it should actually serve (`interfaces-config`); restrict firewalld exposure to the relevant network segment.

Optional hardening: DHCP snooping at the switch layer (network-infrastructure-side, not a RHEL/Kea setting) to prevent rogue servers; careful reservation management to reduce reliance on broad dynamic pools where predictability matters.

p: Kea is a comparatively newer addition to RHEL's supported service set; verify SELinux policy maturity for your specific configuration (especially if using a nonstandard lease-database path or hook libraries) and consult `ausearch`/`sealert` if you encounter denials rather than assuming stock policy covers every possible Kea deployment pattern.

list: Availability: consider Kea's high-availability hook library and/or a database-backed lease store for redundant DHCP service in critical environments.
Reliability: size address pools with adequate headroom for your actual client churn/count.
Security: scope network exposure tightly; coordinate with network team on DHCP snooping to prevent rogue servers.
Monitoring: monitor pool utilization/exhaustion and lease-assignment failure rates.

Configuration management: manage Kea's JSON configuration via configuration management tooling for consistency, and validate JSON syntax as a pre-deploy gate (a malformed JSON file will simply fail to load).
Migration: if migrating from RHEL 8/9 ISC dhcpd, budget real time for `keama`-assisted conversion review and testing — don't treat it as a drop-in swap.

p: DHCP servers are rarely a raw-performance bottleneck at typical enterprise scale; the more common "performance" complaint is actually pool exhaustion or lease-time misconfiguration causing excessive renewal traffic — address the configuration, not the daemon's resource allocation, first.

🟡 Not verifying the exact systemd unit name(s) for Kea on the installed package version before writing automation/documentation around it — this has genuinely varied across Kea releases/packagings.

🟠 Running a second, unauthorized/rogue DHCP server (even accidentally, e.g., a forgotten test VM) on the same broadcast domain as a production DHCP server, causing intermittent client misconfiguration that can be very confusing to diagnose.

title: firewalld
analogy: Think of firewalld as a building's security desk with different zones of trust: "public lobby" (untrusted, minimal access), "employee floor" (internal, more access), "server room" (trusted, broad access). Every network interface (front door, side door) is assigned to one of these zones, and the desk enforces a different rule set per zone rather than one global rule for the whole building.

sections.code:
Client
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Interface → bound to a firewalld ZONE (via NetworkManager)
   ↓
firewalld runtime ruleset (nftables backend)
   ↓
Zone rules: services / ports / rich rules / masquerade / port-forwarding
   ↓
Port reached (or dropped/rejected per zone policy)
   ↓
Application-layer socket (bound by the target service)
   ↓
SELinux (port-type context checked independently — see Section 11)
   ↓
Data

rpm -q firewalld                # 🟢
sudo dnf install firewalld      # 🟡 (present by default on nearly all installs)
firewall-cmd --version          # 🟢

p: firewalld's own reload is usually driven via `firewall-cmd`, not `systemctl`:

start vs enable / stop vs disable / restart vs reload: same general systemd semantics as Profile 1, but for firewalld specifically prefer `firewall-cmd --reload` over `systemctl restart firewalld` for applying new permanent rules — it is the officially supported "apply my saved config" action and is less disruptive.
sections.code:
systemctl status firewalld
systemctl start firewalld
systemctl stop firewalld           # 🔴 removes all firewalld-managed protection immediately
systemctl restart firewalld        # 🟠 brief rule-table rebuild; existing connections may be affected depending on backend/tracking state
systemctl reload firewalld         # 🟡 firewalld's own "reload" concept is closer to firewall-cmd --reload (see below) — the systemd-level reload re-reads config similarly without a full daemon restart
systemctl enable firewalld
systemctl disable firewalld        # 🔴 do not disable in production without a compensating control
systemctl is-active firewalld
systemctl is-enabled firewalld

firewall-cmd --reload              # 🟠 applies permanent config to runtime; brief rule-table swap, existing tracked connections generally survive
firewall-cmd --complete-reload     # 🔴 full reinitialization, including breaking tracked connections — use only when --reload isn't sufficient

list: Defaults (do not edit): `/usr/lib/firewalld/` — zones, services, icmptypes shipped by the package.
Administrator overrides (edit here): `/etc/firewalld/` — mirrors the same structure; files here take priority over `/usr/lib/firewalld/`.
Main daemon config: `/etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf` — sets `DefaultZone`, `FirewallBackend` (nftables by default on RHEL 10), logging options.
Zone files: `/etc/firewalld/zones/ZONENAME.xml`
Service definitions: `/etc/firewalld/services/SERVICENAME.xml`

Runtime state: held in firewalld's memory / the live nftables ruleset — not a flat file; inspect via `firewall-cmd`, not by reading nft tables directly (though `nft list ruleset` (🟢) will show firewalld's tables for advanced diagnosis).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`DefaultZone` (firewalld.conf) — Zone assigned to interfaces with no explicit zone — `DefaultZone=public` — New interfaces default to the restrictive `public` zone
`FirewallBackend` (firewalld.conf) — Which kernel packet-filter API firewalld drives — `FirewallBackend=nftables` — RHEL 10 default; `iptables` is legacy/deprecated

`target` (in a zone XML) — Default action for unmatched traffic in that zone — `target="DROP"` (silent) vs `target="REJECT"` vs `target="ACCEPT"` — Determines whether unmatched connections are silently dropped, actively rejected, or allowed

p: firewalld doesn't own a fixed port itself (it's a control daemon over the kernel firewall). Its job is to control other services' reachability.
Verifying listening sockets and firewall rules together:

Distinguish clearly: a port can be (a) listening locally (`ss`), (b) allowed through firewalld, and (c) actually reachable from a remote host — all three must be true; test reachability from a different host, not just `curl localhost`.
list: Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
N/A — N/A — firewalld itself has no listening network port — D-Bus (local only) is how `firewall-cmd` talks to the daemon
sections.code:
ss -lntup                                    # 🟢 what's actually listening on the host
firewall-cmd --list-all                      # 🟢 what firewalld currently allows in the active zone
firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-ports      # 🟢
firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-services   # 🟢

list: Service dependencies: systemd; effectively no dependency on other RHEL daemons to function, though it must start early to protect the host during boot.
Network dependencies: NetworkManager for interface-to-zone binding (Profile 2) — a mismatch between the two is a very common source of "wrong zone" bugs.
Storage dependencies: none beyond normal root filesystem for `/etc/firewalld/`.
Authentication dependencies: none directly; `firewall-cmd` privileged operations require root/Polkit.
Security dependencies: works alongside, not instead of, SELinux — both must independently permit a connection (see Sections 11–12 in every network-service profile in this handbook).
Configuration dependencies: runtime vs. permanent split (Section 2) — a change without `--permanent` is lost on reload/reboot; a `--permanent` change without `--reload` isn't active yet.

p: Objective: Open TCP port 8080 permanently in the `public` zone for a custom application.
Verification:
Expected result: remote clients can now reach port 8080 (assuming SELinux also permits it if relevant, and the app is bound to a non-loopback address).
Objective: Add a named service (e.g., http) rather than a raw port, for readability and to inherit any protocol-specific ICMP handling.
Objective: Test a change safely before making it permanent.
sections.code:
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent   # 🟡 writes to disk, not yet active
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                                        # 🟠 activates it

firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-ports        # 🟢 confirm 8080/tcp present
ss -lntup | grep 8080                          # 🟢 confirm the app is actually listening

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent   # 🟡
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                                       # 🟠

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp    # 🟡 runtime only — reverts on reload/reboot automatically if it breaks something
# test it...
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent   # 🟡 only after confirming it works
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

list: Authentication/Authorization: changing firewalld state requires root or Polkit-delegated privilege.
Least privilege: open only the specific ports/services actually required; prefer named services (which Red Hat maintains) over broad port ranges.
Network exposure: the `public` zone is the RHEL 10 default for new interfaces and only permits SSH + DHCPv6-client by default — a deliberately conservative starting point.
Firewall requirements: none beyond firewalld's own presence and correct zone assignment.
Sensitive files: zone/service XML files under `/etc/firewalld/` reveal your access policy — protect from unauthorized read/write, though this is a lower-sensitivity concern than credential files.
Logging/Auditing: `LogDenied` in `firewalld.conf` can log dropped/rejected packets for specific zones — useful for security monitoring, but adds log volume.
Required security configuration: keep a restrictive default zone; do not set `target="ACCEPT"` on an internet-facing zone.
Optional hardening: rich rules with source-IP restriction for management ports (SSH, database ports) rather than opening them to the whole zone.
Never disable firewalld as the "normal" way to fix a connectivity problem — diagnose the specific zone/port/service mismatch instead.

p: firewalld and SELinux are independent, both-must-agree controls. Opening a port in firewalld does not make SELinux permit a process to bind to it if that port isn't labeled for the expected service type.

A very common real-world failure: a web app is moved to a nonstandard port, firewalld is opened for it, but SELinux still only permits `httpd_t` to bind the standard `http_port_t` set — the fix is `semanage port -a`, not disabling SELinux.
sections.code:
getenforce
sestatus
semanage port -l | grep http_port_t         # 🟢 list ports SELinux associates with a given type
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 # 🟡 label a non-standard port for an SELinux-aware service (e.g., httpd)
getsebool -a | grep httpd                   # 🟢 list relevant booleans
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on   # 🟡 persistent boolean change
ausearch -m avc -ts recent                  # 🟢 find recent denials

p: (This section is folded into the profile's core content above/below since firewalld is the subject; other profiles reference back to this one.)

Zones: predefined trust levels (`drop`, `block`, `public`, `external`, `dmz`, `work`, `home`, `internal`, `trusted`) — each with different default target/behavior; `public` is the RHEL default. Interfaces/sources: an interface or a source IP/subnet can be assigned to a zone; source-based zone assignment lets you treat specific IPs specially regardless of which interface they arrive on. Runtime vs. permanent: the single most important operational distinction — always decide deliberately whether a change should be temporary (test) or permanent (`--permanent` + `--reload`). Common zone mistakes: assuming a `--permanent` change is already active (it isn't, until `--reload`); assuming a runtime-only change survives a reboot (it doesn't); configuring the wrong zone because NetworkManager has the interface in a different zone than assumed — always check `--get-active-zones` first.
sections.code:
firewall-cmd --state                          # 🟢 running or not
firewall-cmd --get-active-zones               # 🟢 which zones are bound to which interfaces/sources right now
firewall-cmd --list-all                       # 🟢 full detail for the default zone
firewall-cmd --list-all-zones                 # 🟢 every zone's full config
firewall-cmd --list-services                  # 🟢
firewall-cmd --list-ports                     # 🟢

Correlate firewalld's own service log with SELinux AVC denials (`ausearch`) — a connection can fail at either layer independently.

Security: combine firewalld with SELinux and, where applicable, an upstream network firewall/security group — defense in depth.

Configuration management: manage zone/service XML and `firewalld.conf` via configuration management tooling; avoid ad hoc runtime-only changes in production that aren't captured anywhere.

p: firewalld/nftables rule evaluation is rarely the performance bottleneck on typical server workloads, but very large rich-rule sets can add latency:

If firewalld/nftables is genuinely implicated in a performance problem, it is almost always due to an excessive number of individually-managed rich rules rather than the framework itself — consolidate where possible.

🟡 Running a change without `--permanent`, then being surprised it's gone after a reboot or `--reload`.

title: libvirt / KVM / QEMU
analogy: Think of KVM as the physical land a housing development is built on (the kernel-level capability that makes efficient virtualization possible at all), QEMU as the actual house-construction crew building and furnishing each individual house (a VM's emulated hardware — disks, NICs, video, etc.), and libvirt as the property management company you actually call to request a new house be built, torn down, started, or stopped — you rarely deal directly with the construction crew (QEMU) yourself.

sections.code:
Administrator (virsh / virt-install / virt-manager / Cockpit)
   ↓
libvirt API (modular daemons: virtqemud, virtnetworkd, virtstoraged, etc.)
   ↓
Domain XML definition (per-VM configuration: CPU, memory, disks, NICs, etc.)
   ↓
QEMU process (per running VM) — device emulation
   ↓
KVM kernel module — hardware-accelerated CPU/memory virtualization (requires Intel VT-x / AMD-V)
   ↓
Physical CPU virtualization extensions
   ↓
Guest OS running inside the VM

p: If `virt-host-validate` reports a FAIL for hardware virtualization, VMs will generally fail to boot (rather than merely run slowly) unless a QEMU-only emulation domain type is explicitly (and, per Red Hat, unsupportedly) configured — this is not a viable production workaround.
sections.code:
lscpu | grep -i virtualization        # 🟢 confirm hardware virtualization support (VT-x/AMD-V) BEFORE installing anything
grep -cE 'vmx|svm' /proc/cpuinfo      # 🟢 alternative check
sudo dnf install qemu-kvm libvirt virt-install virt-viewer    # 🟡 Red Hat's documented minimal package set for RHEL 10
sudo virt-host-validate                # 🟢 comprehensive pre-flight check for virtualization readiness

p: For a system upgraded from an older monolithic-`libvirtd` setup:
Per-VM lifecycle (via `virsh`, not systemctl):
sections.code:
sudo systemctl enable --now virtqemud.socket   # verify exact unit names for your version first
systemctl status virtqemud
systemctl status virtnetworkd

systemctl status libvirtd     # may still be present/relevant depending on your migration path — verify which model is actually active

virsh list --all                 # 🟢 list all VMs and their state
virsh start VMNAME                # 🟡 boots a defined VM
virsh shutdown VMNAME             # 🟡 graceful guest shutdown (requires guest ACPI/agent support)
virsh destroy VMNAME              # 🟠 hard power-off — equivalent to pulling the power cord, use only when graceful shutdown isn't working
virsh reboot VMNAME               # 🟡 graceful guest reboot
virsh undefine VMNAME             # 🔴 removes the VM's definition (NOT its disk by default — but combined with --remove-all-storage it IS destructive)

list: Per-VM domain definitions: stored internally by libvirt (typically under `/etc/libvirt/qemu/*.xml`) — edit via `virsh edit VMNAME`, not by hand-editing the XML file directly while libvirt is running, to avoid state desync.
Storage pool definitions: `/etc/libvirt/storage/*.xml`; default VM disk image location commonly `/var/lib/libvirt/images/`.
Network definitions: `/etc/libvirt/qemu/networks/*.xml` (the default NAT-based `default` network is commonly pre-defined).
libvirt daemon config: `/etc/libvirt/virtqemud.conf` (or `libvirtd.conf` on the legacy monolithic model).
Logs: `/var/log/libvirt/qemu/VMNAME.log` (per-VM QEMU log) plus journald for the libvirt daemon(s) themselves.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`<domain type='kvm'>` (in domain XML) — Specifies KVM-accelerated virtualization — (default for `virt-install` when hardware support is present) — Uses hardware-accelerated virtualization; `type='qemu'` (software-only emulation) is a Red-Hat-unsupported fallback with severe performance implications, not a production option
`<memory>` / `<vcpu>` — Resource allocation — `<memory unit='GiB'>4</memory>` — Defines the VM's allocated RAM/CPU count

`<source network='default'/>` (in a NIC device definition) — Which libvirt network a VM's NIC attaches to — (as shown) — Determines the VM's network connectivity model (NAT via the default network, or a bridged/other configuration for more direct host-network access)

p: libvirt's own management API is typically local (Unix socket) by default, not network-exposed, unless explicitly configured for remote management (e.g., over SSH tunneling — the common, recommended remote-management pattern — or, less commonly and with more careful security consideration, TLS-secured TCP).

VM-specific network traffic (whatever the guest OS itself does) is governed by the guest's own configuration and the host's `libvirt` network/bridge setup — treat any given VM's exposed services according to that VM's own relevant profile in this handbook (e.g., if a VM runs httpd, Profile 11's guidance applies inside that guest).
list: Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
N/A (local socket, default) — — — Local libvirt API access — Default and recommended for single-host management
SSH-tunneled (`qemu+ssh://`) — TCP 22 (reuses SSH, Profile 4) — Recommended remote management pattern — Inherits SSH's own security posture — no separate exposure

TLS (`qemu+tls://`, if configured) — TCP 16514 (conventional) — Direct remote management without SSH tunneling — Requires proper certificate infrastructure; more exposure surface than SSH tunneling if misconfigured
Service dependencies: the kernel KVM module (`kvm_intel`/`kvm_amd`) must be loaded; libvirt's modular daemons depend on systemd socket activation in modern configurations.
Network dependencies: the `default` NAT network (or a configured bridge) for VM connectivity; firewalld considerations if remote/TLS-based management is used.
Storage dependencies: adequate space in the configured storage pool location for VM disk images.
Authentication dependencies: Polkit for local access control to libvirt operations; SSH (for `qemu+ssh://` remote management, Profile 4) or TLS certificates (for `qemu+tls://`).

Security dependencies: SELinux's sVirt subsystem, which assigns each running VM's QEMU process a unique dynamic SELinux context/category, isolating VMs from each other even if one is compromised — analogous in spirit to Podman's per-container MCS labeling (Profile 18).
Configuration dependencies: correct domain XML (edited via `virsh edit`, validated by libvirt itself on save).

Verification:
Objective: Gracefully shut down and later start a VM.
sections.code:
sudo virt-install \
  --name myvm \

  --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/myvm.qcow2,size=20 \
