list: Authentication/Authorization: Polkit governs local libvirt API access; remote access should go through SSH tunneling (`qemu+ssh://`) or properly configured TLS — never an unauthenticated network-exposed libvirt API.

Least privilege: run VMs with only the resources/devices they actually need (avoid unnecessary device passthrough); prefer the `default` isolated/NAT network unless bridged/direct network access is specifically required.

VM isolation: sVirt (SELinux-based) assigns each VM a unique, dynamically generated security context, meaning even if one VM's QEMU process were compromised, SELinux policy prevents it from accessing another VM's resources — a foundational, default-on security feature, not something to disable.
Network exposure: don't expose libvirt's management API directly to untrusted networks; use SSH tunneling as the default remote-management pattern.
Sensitive files: VM disk images (may contain sensitive guest data), any TLS certificates used for remote management.
Required security configuration: sVirt/SELinux enabled (default); local-socket-only or SSH-tunneled remote management.
Optional hardening: TLS-based remote management with proper certificate infrastructure for larger/multi-admin environments; disk image encryption for sensitive guest data at rest.

p: A common SELinux+libvirt issue: manually copying a VM disk image into the images directory (rather than letting libvirt/`virt-install` create it) can leave it with an incorrect label, preventing the VM from starting — `restorecon -Rv /var/lib/libvirt/images/` resolves typical cases.
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep qemu-kvm             # each running VM's QEMU process shows a UNIQUE sVirt category (e.g., system_u:system_r:svirt_t:s0:c123,c456) — this uniqueness per VM is sVirt's core isolation mechanism
ls -Z /var/lib/libvirt/images/    # expect svirt_image_t (or similarly labeled) contexts on VM disk images
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c qemu-kvm

p: For the far more common SSH-tunneled remote management pattern, no additional firewalld rule beyond SSH itself (Profile 4) is needed. For VM-level network exposure (e.g., a bridged VM running its own services), firewalld considerations apply inside the guest per that guest's own OS and services, not on the host's firewalld for libvirt itself.
sections.code:
firewall-cmd --list-services | grep libvirt    # generally NOT needed for local-only management
firewall-cmd --add-service=libvirt-tls --permanent   # 🟡 only if using qemu+tls:// remote management
firewall-cmd --reload                                 # 🟠

journalctl -u virtqemud                   # 🟢 (verify exact unit name) libvirt daemon lifecycle events
cat /var/log/libvirt/qemu/VMNAME.log      # 🟢 per-VM QEMU process log — the first place to check for a specific VM's boot/runtime issues
virsh dommemstat VMNAME                    # 🟢 live memory statistics

virt-host-validate                # overall virtualization readiness
systemctl is-active virtqemud     # (verify exact unit name)
virsh list --all
virsh dominfo VMNAME
lsmod | grep kvm                   # confirm the KVM kernel module is loaded

list: Availability: consider live migration capability (moving a running VM between hosts) for planned maintenance without guest downtime, where infrastructure supports it.
Reliability: always prefer `virsh shutdown` (graceful) over `virsh destroy` (hard) for planned VM stops.
Security: never disable sVirt/SELinux VM isolation; use SSH-tunneled or TLS-secured remote management only.
Monitoring: monitor host resource oversubscription (CPU/RAM allocated across VMs versus physical capacity) and per-VM resource usage (`virsh dommemstat`, `virt-top` if installed).

Configuration management: manage VM domain definitions and libvirt network/storage pool definitions via configuration management/automation (e.g., `virt-install` scripting, or higher-level orchestration) for consistency at scale.

Disaster recovery: back up VM disk images and their domain XML definitions (`virsh dumpxml VMNAME > backup.xml`) separately, so a VM can be fully reconstructed even if libvirt's internal state is lost.

p: VM performance issues are frequently host-level resource oversubscription (too many VMs' allocated resources exceeding physical capacity) rather than a defect in any single VM's configuration — check host-wide utilization before tuning an individual VM.
sections.code:
virt-top                          # 🟢 (if installed) top-like view across all VMs
virsh dommemstat VMNAME           # 🟢 per-VM memory statistics
virsh domstats VMNAME              # 🟢 broader per-VM statistics (CPU, block I/O, network)
top / vmstat (on the HOST)         # 🟢 overall host resource pressure across all VMs combined
iostat -x 1                        # 🟢 host storage I/O if VM disk performance is in question

Install the virtualization package set; identify actual libvirt daemon unit names on your system.

failures.fix: 🔴 Attempting virtualization on hardware/hypervisor-nested environments without confirming `virt-host-validate` passes first — a FAIL for hardware virtualization means VMs won't boot at all, not just "run slowly."
🟡 Hand-editing a VM's XML file directly on disk while libvirt is running instead of using `virsh edit` — can cause state desync between libvirt's internal view and the file.
🟡 Manually copying disk images into the images directory without correct SELinux labeling, causing VM start failures.
🟠 Using `virsh destroy` (hard power-off) as a routine shutdown method instead of `virsh shutdown` (graceful) — risks guest filesystem corruption just as pulling a physical machine's power cord would.

title: NFS
analogy: Think of NFS as a shared filing cabinet in a central office (the server) that satellite offices (clients) can access remotely as if it were sitting in their own building — an employee at a client site opens what looks like a local folder, but every read/write actually travels over the network to the real cabinet.

sections.code:
Client application (reads/writes files normally)
   ↓
Kernel NFS client (translates to NFS protocol calls)
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP/UDP 2049 (NFSv4; NFSv3 additionally needs rpcbind + dynamic/configured ports for mountd/statd)
   ↓
NFS server (kernel nfsd threads + rpc.mountd for mount negotiation)
   ↓
/etc/exports (which paths, to which clients, with what options)
   ↓
Permissions / SELinux (nfs_export_all_rw or similar booleans; standard Unix perms on exported files)
   ↓
Underlying local filesystem on the server (Data)

rpm -q nfs-utils                  # 🟢
sudo dnf install nfs-utils        # 🟡 needed on both server and client roles

p: Server side:
Applying export changes without a full restart (preferred):

Client side: there's typically no single "client service" to restart for an individual mount — mounting/unmounting is managed per-mount (`mount`/`umount`, or via `/etc/fstab`/autofs, Profile 17); `nfs-client.target` groups the relevant support units (`rpc-statd`, `nfs-idmapd`) that do run continuously to support NFS client functionality.
sections.code:
systemctl status nfs-server
systemctl start nfs-server
systemctl stop nfs-server            # 🔴 all clients lose access to exported paths — hung client processes/mounts are likely
systemctl restart nfs-server         # 🟠 briefly interrupts client access; well-behaved NFS clients often recover after a restart, but application-level errors during the gap are possible
systemctl enable nfs-server
systemctl is-active nfs-server

sudo exportfs -ra    # 🟡 re-reads /etc/exports and applies changes to currently running nfsd, without a service restart

list: Exports definition (server): `/etc/exports`, plus drop-ins under `/etc/exports.d/*.exports`.
NFS-wide tuning (server and client): `/etc/nfs.conf` (modern nfs-utils centralizes many settings here rather than the older `/etc/sysconfig/nfs`).
ID mapping (NFSv4): `/etc/idmapd.conf`.
Client-side fstab entries: `/etc/fstab` (`server:/export /mnt/point nfs defaults 0 0`).
Logs: journald under the relevant units; kernel-level NFS messages appear in the kernel log (`journalctl -k`).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`/etc/exports` entry — Defines an export and its client access rules — `/srv/shared 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_root_squash)` — Grants read-write access to that subnet; `no_root_squash` is a significant security relaxation — see Section 10

`sync` vs `async` — Write-commit behavior — `sync` (safer, Red-Hat-recommended default posture) — `sync` waits for writes to reach stable storage before acknowledging — safer against data loss on server crash; `async` is faster but risks silent data loss on a server crash mid-write

`root_squash` (default) vs `no_root_squash` — Whether the remote root user is mapped to an unprivileged user on the server — (default: `root_squash` is implicit/standard for security) — `no_root_squash` lets a client's root user act as root on the server's exported filesystem — a significant privilege-escalation risk if that client isn't fully trusted
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
TCP/UDP — 2049 — NFS data protocol (NFSv4 consolidates most traffic here) — Primary port to allow for NFSv4-only deployments

TCP/UDP — 111 — `rpcbind` (portmapper) — relevant for NFSv3 and some ancillary services — NFSv4-only environments can often minimize/avoid rpcbind dependency, but verify against your actual configuration rather than assuming

Dynamic or configurable — mountd, statd, lockd (NFSv3-era ancillary daemons) — Various NFSv3 support functions — If NFSv3 must be supported, these ports should be pinned to fixed values in `/etc/nfs.conf` for predictable firewalld rules, rather than left dynamic
sections.code:
ss -lntup | grep -E '2049|111'    # 🟢 confirm listening ports match your intended NFS version(s)
rpcinfo -p    # 🟢 (if rpcbind is in use) lists registered RPC services and their ports — useful for NFSv3 troubleshooting

list: Service dependencies: `rpcbind` (for NFSv3/ancillary services), `rpc-statd` (NFSv3 locking recovery).

Network dependencies: firewalld allowing the relevant port(s) for your NFS version(s) in use; DNS/hostname resolution consistency between server and clients (relevant to Kerberos-based NFS security if used).
Storage dependencies: the underlying local filesystem being exported must itself be healthy/mounted before `nfs-server` starts successfully.

Authentication dependencies: by default, NFS relies on the client's own UID/GID assertions (a significant trust assumption — see Security); Kerberos-based `sec=krb5*` options provide stronger authentication where required.

Security dependencies: SELinux booleans (`nfs_export_all_rw`, `nfs_export_all_ro`, `use_nfs_home_dirs`, etc.) frequently need explicit configuration; standard Unix permissions still apply on top of NFS-level export rules.

Configuration dependencies: consistent UID/GID mapping between server and clients (or NFSv4 ID mapping via `idmapd.conf`) — mismatched UIDs are a very common source of "wrong owner" confusion on NFS-mounted files.

p: Objective: Export a directory read-write to a specific subnet.
Verification (server):
Verification (client):
sections.code:
sudo mkdir -p /srv/shared                                        # 🟡
sudo tee -a /etc/exports <<'EOF'
/srv/shared 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,root_squash)
EOF
sudo exportfs -ra                                                 # 🟡 applies without full restart

sudo mount -t nfs SERVER:/srv/shared /mnt/test    # 🟡

list: Authentication: default NFS trusts the client's asserted UID/GID (`AUTH_SYS`) — meaning any user with root on a permitted client can potentially impersonate any UID unless `root_squash` and careful client trust boundaries are maintained, or Kerberos (`sec=krb5`/`krb5i`/`krb5p`) is used for stronger authentication and optionally integrity/privacy protection.
Authorization: `/etc/exports` client restrictions (by IP/subnet) plus standard Unix file permissions on the exported content.
Privilege requirements: exporting/mounting NFS requires root on both server and client.

Least privilege: always default to `root_squash` (map remote root to an unprivileged user) unless there's a specific, well-understood reason for `no_root_squash`; export read-only wherever write access isn't genuinely required.

Network exposure: NFS traffic is unencrypted by default (`AUTH_SYS`); use Kerberos with `krb5p` (privacy/encryption) for exports crossing untrusted network segments, or restrict NFS to a trusted, segmented network.
Sensitive files: `/etc/exports` itself reveals your storage-sharing topology — protect appropriately.
Required security configuration: `root_squash` by default; export scope limited to specific trusted subnets, never `0.0.0.0/0` equivalents without strong justification.
Optional hardening: Kerberos-based `sec=` options for authentication/encryption in higher-assurance environments.

p: A common real-world pairing: NFS-mounted home directories work for file access but break interactive login features (e.g., certain session/desktop features) until `use_nfs_home_dirs` is enabled.

list: Availability: consider `hard` vs. `soft` mount semantics deliberately — `hard` mounts (the safer default for data integrity) will retry indefinitely and can hang client processes during a server outage; `soft` mounts fail faster but risk silent data corruption on interrupted writes — this is a genuine, consequential trade-off, not a "pick the safer-sounding one" decision.
Reliability: pair with centralized identity (SSSD, Profile 14) to avoid UID/GID drift across a fleet.
Security: default to `root_squash`, minimal export scope, and Kerberos where the network path isn't fully trusted.
Monitoring: monitor `nfs-server` health and export availability; monitor for client-side mount hangs.
Configuration management: manage `/etc/exports` and client-side `/etc/fstab`/autofs maps centrally for consistency.
Disaster recovery: back up the underlying exported filesystem itself (NFS is just the sharing layer) per standard backup practice for that storage.

p: NFS performance issues are frequently underlying storage or network latency issues surfacing through the NFS layer rather than an NFS-specific defect — correlate `nfsstat` findings with the server's actual disk I/O and network conditions before assuming an NFS-layer tuning problem.

title: OpenSSH / sshd
analogy: Think of sshd as a building's front desk that checks ID (authentication) before issuing a keycard (an encrypted session) to a specific floor (the user's shell/permissions) — and every conversation through that keycard is inside a locked, soundproofed tube (encryption) so nobody in the hallway can listen in or tamper with it.

sections.code:
Client (ssh)
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP/22 (or custom Port)
   ↓
sshd listening socket
   ↓
sshd_config (host keys, ciphers, auth methods allowed)
   ↓
Authentication (public key / password via PAM, possibly SSSD-backed)
   ↓
Permissions / SELinux (sshd_t context, user shell, home directory contexts)
   ↓
Shell / SFTP subsystem / forwarded channel (Data)

rpm -q openssh-server                    # 🟢
sudo dnf install openssh-server          # 🟡 (present by default on nearly all installs)
sshd -V                                  # 🟢 note: prints to stderr, shows version + compiled-in features
ssh -V                                   # 🟢 client version

p: restart vs reload — this matters more for sshd than almost any other service: existing interactive sessions are separate child processes and are NOT killed by either `restart` or `reload` — but `restart` briefly closes and reopens the listening socket, so if your `sshd_config` has an error, `restart` can leave you with no way to open a new connection (while your current session may still work, precariously). Always validate config before restart (see Section 9) and, ideally, use `reload` for config changes and keep your current session open until you've confirmed a new connection succeeds.
sections.code:
systemctl status sshd
systemctl start sshd
systemctl stop sshd            # 🔴 removes remote access via SSH immediately — never do this without another access path
systemctl restart sshd         # 🟠 drops nothing for already-established sessions (existing connections generally survive a restart since they're independent processes), but stops NEW connections briefly during restart
systemctl reload sshd          # 🟡 re-reads sshd_config for new connections without dropping the listening socket or existing sessions — preferred for config changes
systemctl enable sshd
systemctl disable sshd         # 🔴 do not disable on a server you manage remotely
systemctl is-active sshd
systemctl is-enabled sshd

list: Main config: `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`
Config drop-ins: `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` (included via `Include` directive near the top of `sshd_config` on modern OpenSSH — later files can override earlier directives for most keywords)
Client-side config: `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`, `~/.ssh/config`
Host keys: `/etc/ssh/ssh_host__key` (private, `600`, root-owned) and `.pub` (public)

Per-user keys: `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (must be `600`, `~/.ssh` must be `700`, home directory not group/world-writable, or sshd will refuse to use the key by default — a very common troubleshooting scenario)
Logs: journald under `sshd` unit (traditionally `/var/log/secure` via rsyslog on RHEL — see Profile 10).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`PermitRootLogin` — Whether root can log in directly — `PermitRootLogin no` — Forces admins to log in as a normal user then `sudo`/`su` — standard hardening baseline
`PasswordAuthentication` — Whether password auth is allowed — `PasswordAuthentication no` — Forces key-based auth only — significantly reduces brute-force risk
`Port` — Listening port — `Port 2222` — Changes the port sshd listens on — requires matching firewalld port change AND an SELinux port label change, or the daemon will fail to bind/be reachable
`AllowUsers` / `AllowGroups` — Restrict which accounts may SSH in — `AllowGroups sysadmins` — Denies SSH login to any account not in the allowed group, regardless of valid credentials

p: Changing `Port` requires: (1) updating `sshd_config`, (2) `semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp NEWPORT` (SELinux), (3) `firewall-cmd --add-port=NEWPORT/tcp --permanent && firewall-cmd --reload`, in that order, before restarting sshd — otherwise you can be locked out or the daemon may fail to bind.
list: Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations

TCP — 22 (default; configurable) — SSH protocol (shell, SFTP, port forwarding) — Internet-facing SSH on the default port is a constant scan/brute-force target — consider key-only auth, fail2ban-style rate limiting, and restricting source IPs via firewalld rich rules for management access
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep sshd          # 🟢 confirm listening port and address

list: Service dependencies: systemd; typically ordered after `network.target`.
Network dependencies: a bound, reachable network interface; firewalld allowing the configured port.
Storage dependencies: host key files must exist and be readable only by root; home directories for `authorized_keys`.
Authentication dependencies: PAM (`/etc/pam.d/sshd`); optionally SSSD for centralized identity (Profile 14).
Security dependencies: SELinux `ssh_port_t` labeling for any non-default port; correct file permissions on keys.
Configuration dependencies: `sshd_config` syntax validity (`sshd -t`) before every restart.

Critical practice: keep your current SSH session open and test the change from a new connection before closing the original — this guarantees a rollback path if something is wrong.

sudo sshd -t                                                        # 🟢 validate syntax BEFORE reload

ssh-copy-id user@host                    # 🟡 or manually append to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no user@host   # 🟢 confirm key-based login succeeds

list: Authentication: public key (preferred), password (via PAM, ideally disabled for internet-facing hosts), and optionally certificate-based or multi-factor via PAM modules.
Authorization: `AllowUsers`/`AllowGroups`/`DenyUsers`/`DenyGroups` in `sshd_config`; `sudo`/`su` for privilege escalation after login (never grant direct root SSH as the default posture).
Privilege requirements: sshd itself must start as root (to bind privileged port 22 and read host keys) but drops privileges to the authenticated user's UID for the session.
Least privilege: `PermitRootLogin no`; restrict `AllowGroups` to actual administrators; disable unused authentication methods.
Network exposure: internet-facing SSH should be restricted via firewalld rich rules to known management source ranges where feasible.
Sensitive files: private host keys (`ssh_host__key`, no extension) and every user's `~/.ssh/id_` private keys and `authorized_keys`.

Encryption: modern OpenSSH negotiates strong ciphers/KEX by default; RHEL 10's system-wide crypto policy (`update-crypto-policies`) governs allowed algorithms centrally, including post-quantum key exchange support introduced with RHEL 10 (confirm exact algorithm names/support level with `ssh -Q kex` on your system — I could not verify the precise default PQ KEX algorithm name from a primary Red Hat source at time of writing, so treat that specific detail as unconfirmed pending your own verification).
Logging/Auditing: every login attempt (success/failure) is logged; correlate with `auditd` for compliance requirements around remote access.
Required security configuration: `PermitRootLogin no`, strong `authorized_keys` permissions, host keys never shared across hosts.
Optional hardening: `PasswordAuthentication no`, `AllowGroups`, non-default `Port` (minor obscurity benefit only — not a substitute for the above), fail2ban or equivalent rate-limiting.

p: A classic SELinux+SSH issue: copying `authorized_keys` from a backup/tarball can leave it with the wrong context (e.g., `user_tmp_t` instead of `ssh_home_t`), causing silent public-key auth failures even though permissions (`600`) look correct — `restorecon` fixes it; disabling SELinux does not address the underlying labeling issue and is never the right fix.

Correlate failed logins with `ausearch -m USER_AUTH` / `USER_LOGIN` (auditd, Profile 8) for a compliance-grade audit trail, and with `journalctl -k`/SELinux AVC logs if a key-based login fails for no apparent permission reason.

list: Availability: always test new connections before closing your current session when changing `sshd_config`.
Security: enforce key-only auth, restrict `AllowGroups`, consider certificate-based SSH for fleets, integrate with centralized identity (SSSD) rather than per-host local accounts where feasible.
Monitoring: alert on repeated failed-login spikes (`journalctl`/`auditd`) as a brute-force indicator.
Configuration management: manage `sshd_config`/drop-ins via configuration management with a syntax-check step (`sshd -t`) as a pre-deploy gate.
Disaster recovery: always maintain an out-of-band access path (console, IPMI/iDRAC, cloud provider serial console) as the ultimate rollback for SSH lockouts.

p: SSH itself is rarely a performance bottleneck, but authentication delays are a common complaint:

Slow logins are very often not an sshd problem but an upstream SSSD/LDAP/AD lookup delay (Profile 14) or DNS reverse-lookup delay (`UseDNS` historically caused this; modern defaults typically have it off, verify with `sshd -T | grep usedns`). Use `top`/`ps` to rule out host-level resource exhaustion only after ruling out auth-chain latency.

title: Podman
analogy: Think of Podman as a librarian who checks out books (starts containers) and hands them directly to whoever asked (runs as a normal, traceable child process of your shell/session) — rather than Docker's traditional model of a single central warehouse manager (the dockerd daemon) who holds and manages every book on behalf of everyone, which means Podman has no single central privileged process whose compromise would expose every container on the system.

sections.code:
podman CLI command
   ↓
containers.conf / storage.conf (engine configuration)
   ↓
Image pull/build (via registries.conf-configured sources)
   ↓
crun (OCI runtime) launches the container process
   ↓
conmon (per-container monitor/supervisor process)
   ↓
Namespaces: PID, mount, network (netavark-managed), user (for rootless)
   ↓
cgroups v2 (resource accounting/limits)
   ↓
SELinux (container_t / per-container unique MCS labels for isolation between containers)
   ↓
Running container workload

sudo dnf install podman            # 🟡 (typically pulls in crun/netavark as dependencies)

p: Because Podman is daemonless, there's no single "the Podman service" to start/stop in the traditional sense for basic usage. For systemd-managed containers (the recommended pattern for production/persistent workloads):
For the optional Docker-API-compatible socket service (used by tools expecting a Docker-like remote API):

list: Engine configuration: `/etc/containers/containers.conf` (system-wide) and `~/.config/containers/containers.conf` (per-user, for rootless).
Storage configuration: `/etc/containers/storage.conf` — defines the storage driver (commonly `overlay`) and root storage location.
Registry configuration: `/etc/containers/registries.conf` — which registries Podman searches/trusts by default.
Quadlet unit files (systemd-native container definitions): `/etc/containers/systemd/*.container` (and `.pod`, `.network`, `.volume` for related resource types).
Connections/farms (RHEL 10 — now read-only in containers.conf): actual state lives in `podman.connections.json`, managed only by Podman itself.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`network_backend` (containers.conf) — Which network backend to use — `network_backend = "netavark"` — The RHEL 10 default and only supported option — CNI is no longer available
`runtime` (containers.conf, `[engine]` section) — Which OCI runtime to use — `runtime = "crun"` — The RHEL 10 default — `runc` is no longer packaged
`network_mode` (rootless-relevant) — Rootless networking mode — `pasta` (RHEL 10 default) — Determines how a rootless container's network namespace connects to the host network

p: Podman itself has no fixed listening port; individual containers may publish ports to the host (`-p HOSTPORT:CONTAINERPORT`), at which point that specific mapped port becomes a normal host-level listener subject to the same firewalld/SELinux considerations as any other network service.
sections.code:
podman ps                              # 🟢 shows running containers and their published ports
ss -lntup | grep <mapped-port>         # 🟢 confirm the host-level listener from a published port

list: Service dependencies: `crun` (OCI runtime), `netavark`/`aardvark-dns` (networking), `conmon` (per-container supervision) — all must be correctly installed and matched in version compatibility.
Network dependencies: firewalld allowing any host ports a container publishes; DNS (aardvark-dns provides container-to-container name resolution within a Podman-managed network).
Storage dependencies: sufficient space under the configured storage root (commonly `/var/lib/containers/storage` for rootful, `~/.local/share/containers/storage` for rootless).
Authentication dependencies: registry authentication (`podman login`) for private image registries.

Security dependencies: SELinux container policy (`container_t`, per-container unique MCS categories preventing cross-container interference even if one is compromised); rootless mode's user-namespace mapping (`/etc/subuid`, `/etc/subgid`).

Configuration dependencies: correct `containers.conf`/`storage.conf` alignment with actually-installed components (a mismatch, e.g., a leftover `runtime = "runc"` reference after upgrade, will fail since `runc` is no longer present).

list: Authentication/Authorization: registry authentication via `podman login`; rootless containers run under the invoking user's UID mapped through `/etc/subuid`/`/etc/subgid` ranges, meaningfully limiting what a compromised container process can affect on the host compared to a root-owned daemon model.
Least privilege: prefer rootless Podman wherever the workload permits it — this is Podman's signature security advantage over daemon-based container engines.
Network exposure: only explicitly published container ports become host-reachable; unpublished container ports remain isolated within the container's network namespace.
Firewall requirements: any published port needs the same firewalld allowance as any other host service listening on that port.
Sensitive files: registry credentials (`~/.config/containers/auth.json` or `/run/containers/0/auth.json`), and any secrets mounted into containers.
Required security configuration: run rootless by default unless a specific workload genuinely requires root privileges; keep images from trusted registries only (`registries.conf` scoping).

Optional hardening: SELinux's per-container unique MCS category labeling (on by default) provides isolation even between containers running as the same UID — don't disable this (`--security-opt label=disable`) without a specific, understood reason, since doing so removes a meaningful isolation layer.

p: A very common Podman+SELinux issue: bind-mounting a host directory into a container fails with permission errors despite correct Unix permissions, because the host directory lacks a container-accessible SELinux label. Fix with the `:z` or `:Z` volume-mount suffix (which tells Podman to relabel the directory appropriately) rather than disabling SELinux for the container:
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep conmon               # expect container_t (with a per-container unique MCS range)
ls -Z /var/lib/containers/         # confirm expected container-related contexts
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c conmon

podman run -v /host/data:/container/data:Z ...    # 🟡 :Z = private label (only this container); :z = shared label (multiple containers)

p: Podman/netavark manage container-internal networking and NAT rules themselves; firewalld's role is specifically about the host-level published port, same as any other service in this handbook.
sections.code:
firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent    # 🟡 for any published container port
firewall-cmd --reload                            # 🟠

podman logs CONTAINER_NAME_OR_ID       # 🟢 container's own stdout/stderr
podman logs -f CONTAINER_NAME_OR_ID    # 🟢 follow mode
journalctl -u mycontainer              # 🟢 if managed as a systemd unit (Quadlet/generated unit) — often the more complete picture combining container output with unit lifecycle events

podman info                       # confirms runtime=crun, networkBackend=netavark — the two critical RHEL 10 defaults
podman ps                         # running containers
podman ps -a                      # all containers including stopped
systemctl status CONTAINER_UNIT   # if systemd-managed

list: Availability: use systemd-managed (Quadlet) containers with `Restart=on-failure` for persistent production workloads rather than ad hoc `podman run` invocations.
Security: default to rootless; use `:z`/`:Z` correctly rather than disabling SELinux labeling; scope `registries.conf` to trusted sources.
Monitoring: monitor container health via `podman ps`/`healthcheck` configuration and the managing systemd unit's status.
Configuration management: manage Quadlet unit files and `containers.conf`/`storage.conf` via configuration management for fleet consistency, especially post-RHEL-10-migration.
Disaster recovery: back up Quadlet definitions and any persistent volumes; container images themselves should be re-pullable from a registry rather than treated as the backup target.

sections.code:
podman stats                    # 🟢 live per-container CPU/memory/network/block I/O usage
top / ps aux | grep conmon       # 🟢 host-level view of container supervisor processes
systemd-cgtop                    # 🟢 (Profile 1) cgroup-level resource view, since Podman containers are cgroup-managed

title: PostgreSQL
analogy: Think of PostgreSQL as a highly organized, meticulous librarian for structured data: every piece of information (row) lives in a strictly defined catalog (table/schema), the librarian enforces strict rules about what can be added or changed (constraints, transactions), and every transaction either fully completes or is entirely rolled back — there's no such thing as a half-shelved book.

sections.code:
Client application (via libpq, psql, or an application driver)
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP 5432
   ↓
postgres (postmaster) listening socket
   ↓
pg_hba.conf (client authentication rules — WHO may connect, HOW, from WHERE)
   ↓
postgresql.conf (server-wide tuning/behavior settings)
   ↓
Per-connection backend process
   ↓
Shared buffers / WAL (write-ahead log) for durability
   ↓
Data files on disk (the PostgreSQL "cluster"/data directory)

rpm -q postgresql-server                  # 🟢
sudo dnf install postgresql-server        # 🟡
postgres --version                         # 🟢 (or: rpm -q postgresql-server, more reliable if postgres isn't yet on $PATH for your shell)

p: A PostgreSQL-specific first step not required by most other services in this handbook — initializing the data directory:
sections.code:
sudo postgresql-setup --initdb    # 🟡 REQUIRED once, before the first start — creates the initial data directory/cluster

systemctl status postgresql
systemctl start postgresql
systemctl stop postgresql            # 🔴 all client connections/application functionality depending on this database stop immediately
systemctl restart postgresql         # 🟠 drops all active connections; applications must reconnect
systemctl reload postgresql          # 🟡 re-reads postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf for settings that support reload (many, but not all — some require a full restart, e.g., changes to shared_buffers) without dropping existing connections
systemctl enable postgresql
systemctl is-active postgresql

p: Located within the PostgreSQL data directory (commonly `/var/lib/pgsql/data/` on RHEL, though exact path can vary by installation method):
list: Server configuration: `postgresql.conf` — connection limits, memory settings (`shared_buffers`, etc.), logging, WAL settings.

Client authentication: `pg_hba.conf` ("host-based authentication") — defines which hosts/users/databases may connect and via which authentication method. This file is critical and frequently misunderstood — see Section 10.
Logs: typically under `<data_directory>/log/` (path/format configurable via `postgresql.conf`), plus journald for the service unit's own lifecycle events.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`listen_addresses` (postgresql.conf) — Which network interfaces to listen on — `listen_addresses = 'localhost'` (default, restrictive) vs `'*'` (all interfaces) — Determines whether PostgreSQL accepts connections beyond localhost at all — a prerequisite for any remote client access, independent of `pg_hba.conf`

`pg_hba.conf` entry — Per-connection-type authentication rule — `host mydb myuser 192.168.1.0/24 scram-sha-256` — Allows `myuser` to connect to `mydb` from that subnet using SCRAM-SHA-256 password authentication
`max_connections` — Connection limit — `max_connections = 100` — Caps concurrent client connections; requires a full restart to change
`shared_buffers` — Memory allocated for PostgreSQL's own data cache — `shared_buffers = 1GB` — A key performance-tuning setting; requires a full restart to change
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations

TCP — 5432 — PostgreSQL client protocol — Restrict via firewalld to only the application hosts/subnets that genuinely need database access; never expose directly to the internet without strong justification and hardening
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep postgres    # 🟢 confirm listening address/port

list: Service dependencies: systemd; the data directory must be initialized (`postgresql-setup --initdb`) before first start.
Network dependencies: firewalld allowing 5432 from intended client sources; `listen_addresses` configured appropriately for the intended access pattern.
Storage dependencies: adequate space for the data directory, including WAL growth under write-heavy workloads; correct ownership (`postgres` user) and permissions on the data directory.

Authentication dependencies: `pg_hba.conf` rules; optionally SSSD/LDAP/Kerberos integration for centralized authentication in larger deployments (verify current PostgreSQL support/configuration for your chosen method).
Security dependencies: SELinux `postgresql_t`/`postgresql_db_t` contexts; TLS configuration for encrypted client connections (`ssl = on` in `postgresql.conf` plus certificate configuration).
Configuration dependencies: `listen_addresses` AND `pg_hba.conf` must BOTH permit a given connection — a very common point of confusion (see Section 10/16).

p: Objective: Initialize and start PostgreSQL for the first time.
Objective: Allow remote application connections to a specific database.
Verification:
sections.code:
sudo postgresql-setup --initdb           # 🟡 one-time
sudo systemctl enable --now postgresql   # 🟡
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT version();"    # 🟢 confirm basic functionality

sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER USER myuser WITH PASSWORD 'a-strong-password';"   # 🟡
sudo tee -a /var/lib/pgsql/data/postgresql.conf <<'EOF'    # 🟡 (verify exact data directory path)
listen_addresses = '*'
EOF
sudo tee -a /var/lib/pgsql/data/pg_hba.conf <<'EOF'         # 🟡
host    mydb    myuser    192.168.1.0/24    scram-sha-256
EOF
sudo systemctl restart postgresql          # 🟠 required for listen_addresses; pg_hba.conf alone would only need reload
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=postgresql --permanent    # 🟡
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                                 # 🟠

ss -lntup | grep postgres                        # 🟢 confirm listening on the expected address
psql -h SERVER_IP -U myuser -d mydb -c "SELECT 1;"   # 🟢 test from a REMOTE client, not just localhost

list: Authentication: governed by `pg_hba.conf` — supports multiple methods (`trust` — no password, dangerous outside tightly controlled local contexts; `password`/`md5` — legacy, weaker; `scram-sha-256` — current recommended method; `peer`/`ident` — OS-user-based, for local connections; certificate-based; and others).
Authorization: PostgreSQL's own role-based permission system (`GRANT`/`REVOKE`) governs what an authenticated user may actually do once connected — a separate layer from authentication.
Privilege requirements: the `postgres` OS user owns the data directory and runs the server process; database-level roles are entirely separate from OS-level users/groups.
Least privilege: grant application database users only the specific privileges they need (avoid routinely using the `postgres` superuser role for application connections).
Network exposure: `listen_addresses` and firewalld together control network exposure; restrict both to only what's actually needed.
Sensitive files: `pg_hba.conf` (reveals authentication policy), and any TLS private keys if SSL is configured.
Required security configuration: `scram-sha-256` (or better) rather than legacy `md5`/`trust` methods for any non-fully-trusted-local context; TLS for connections crossing untrusted network segments.
Optional hardening: row-level security policies for multi-tenant applications; connection limits per role to prevent resource exhaustion by a single misbehaving client.
Never use `trust` authentication for network-reachable connections — it accepts any claimed username with no password verification whatsoever.

p: Moving the data directory to a nonstandard location without corresponding SELinux fcontext definition (`semanage fcontext -a -t postgresql_db_t "PATH(/.*)?"` + `restorecon`) is the most common SELinux-related PostgreSQL issue.
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep postgres                     # expect postgresql_t
ls -Z /var/lib/pgsql/data/                # expect postgresql_db_t
semanage port -l | grep postgresql_port_t # confirm port labeling if using a nonstandard port
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c postgres

firewall-cmd --list-services | grep postgresql
firewall-cmd --add-service=postgresql --permanent   # 🟡
firewall-cmd --reload                                # 🟠

journalctl -u postgresql                       # 🟢 service lifecycle events
tail -f /var/lib/pgsql/data/log/*.log          # 🟢 (verify exact log path/naming per your postgresql.conf settings) actual query/error logging
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW log_directory;" # 🟢 confirm the actual configured log location

systemctl is-active postgresql
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT version();"
ss -lntup | grep postgres
firewall-cmd --list-services
getenforce

list: Availability: consider streaming replication/standby servers for high-availability requirements (beyond this profile's introductory scope — consult current PostgreSQL HA documentation for your version).

Performance: tune `shared_buffers`, `work_mem`, `max_connections`, and connection pooling (e.g., via PgBouncer, an external tool) deliberately based on actual workload characteristics, not generic guesses.
Security: `scram-sha-256` minimum for authentication; TLS for network connections; least-privilege role design.
Monitoring: monitor connection counts, query performance (slow-query logging), disk space (especially WAL growth), and replication lag if applicable.
Backup: implement regular `pg_dump`/`pg_basebackup`-based backups appropriate to your recovery-point/recovery-time objectives (see Section 20).
Configuration management: manage `postgresql.conf`/`pg_hba.conf` via configuration management for fleet consistency, with careful review of any `pg_hba.conf` change given its security significance.

p: Slow queries are frequently a missing-index or poor-query-plan issue (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the specific query) rather than a server-wide tuning problem — diagnose at the query level before broadly retuning server-wide memory settings.
sections.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity;"   # 🟢 current connections/queries
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables;"  # 🟢 table-level activity statistics
top / ps aux | grep postgres    # 🟢 per-backend-process resource usage
iostat -x 1                      # 🟢 underlying storage I/O, often the actual bottleneck for database workloads

🔴 Using `trust` authentication for a network-reachable connection — no password is verified at all.
🟡 Forgetting that `pg_hba.conf` rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins — a broad early rule can shadow a more specific later one in unexpected ways.
🟡 Changing `shared_buffers`/`max_connections` and expecting `reload` to apply it — these require a full `restart`.
🟡 Forgetting `postgresql-setup --initdb` on a fresh install, then being confused why `systemctl start` fails.
🟡 Using the `postgres` superuser role for routine application connections instead of a scoped, least-privilege application role.
🟡 Not planning for WAL growth under write-heavy workloads, leading to unexpected disk-space exhaustion.

title: rsyslog
analogy: Think of rsyslog as a mail-sorting facility: messages (log lines) arrive tagged with a facility (what subsystem generated it — e.g., `auth`, `cron`, `mail`) and a priority (severity — e.g., `info`, `warning`, `err`), and rsyslog's rules decide which "mailbox" (file, remote server, or other destination) each tagged message gets routed to, based on administrator-defined selector rules.

sections.code:
Log sources: systemd-journald (imjournal) / local syslog-protocol senders (/dev/log) / remote senders (network)
   ↓
rsyslogd
   ↓
Rule evaluation (facility.priority selectors, or RainerScript filters)
   ↓
   ├── /var/log/messages (general)
   ├── /var/log/secure (auth-related — see Profile 4's sshd logging)
   ├── /var/log/maillog, /var/log/cron, etc. (facility-specific)
   └── Remote forwarding (UDP/TCP 514, or TLS-wrapped) to a central log collector
   ↓
logrotate (scheduled rotation of the flat files)

rpm -q rsyslog                  # 🟢 present by default on nearly all installs
sudo dnf install rsyslog        # 🟡 rarely needed
rsyslogd -v                     # 🟢 version and compiled-in module info

systemctl status rsyslog
systemctl start rsyslog
systemctl stop rsyslog            # 🟠 traditional flat-file logging stops (journald, Profile 6, continues independently)
systemctl restart rsyslog         # 🟠 brief gap in flat-file logging during restart
systemctl reload rsyslog          # 🟡 re-reads configuration; check `systemctl cat rsyslog` to confirm ExecReload behavior on your version
systemctl enable rsyslog
systemctl disable rsyslog         # 🟠 do not disable if any tooling/compliance process depends on flat-file logs or remote forwarding
systemctl is-active rsyslog
systemctl is-enabled rsyslog

list: Main config: `/etc/rsyslog.conf`
Drop-ins: `/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf`
Log output files: `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/secure`, `/var/log/maillog`, `/var/log/cron`, and others as configured by facility.
Rotation config: `/etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog` (rotation itself is handled by `logrotate`, typically cron/systemd-timer-triggered, not by rsyslog directly).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`module(load="imjournal")` — Ingest from the systemd journal — (default in modern RHEL configs) — rsyslog reads structured journal entries rather than listening on `/dev/log` directly for most local traffic

`facility.priority destination` (traditional selector syntax) — Route matching messages — `authpriv.*  /var/log/secure` — All `authpriv` facility messages, any priority, go to `/var/log/secure` — this is how SSH auth events (Profile 4) land there

`. @@remote-syslog.example.com:514` — Forward all messages to a remote collector — (TCP, `@@`; UDP would be single `@`) — Centralizes logs off-host; `@@` (TCP) is more reliable than `@` (UDP) for forwarding, at the cost of connection-oriented overhead
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
UDP — 514 — Traditional syslog forwarding (unreliable, no delivery guarantee) — Plaintext by default — avoid over untrusted networks without additional protection
TCP — 514 — Reliable syslog forwarding — Still plaintext unless TLS-wrapped
TCP — 6514 (common convention, verify your deployment) — Syslog over TLS (RFC 5425) — Preferred for forwarding across untrusted networks or when confidentiality/integrity of log data matters
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep rsyslog     # 🟢 only relevant if rsyslog is configured to LISTEN (i.e., acting as a collector) — a pure forwarding client has no listening socket for this purpose

list: Service dependencies: typically ordered to start after `systemd-journald` (Profile 6), since `imjournal` reads from it.
Network dependencies: DNS/reachability to any configured remote forwarding destination.
Storage dependencies: `/var/log/` must have adequate space; `imjournal` also maintains its own state file to track journal read position — verify its location/health if forwarding gaps are suspected.
Authentication dependencies: TLS-based forwarding may depend on certificate infrastructure.
Security dependencies: SELinux `syslogd_t` context; firewalld rules if operating as a remote collector (inbound 514/6514).

Configuration dependencies: correct facility/priority selector syntax; rule ordering matters in traditional selector-based configs (later matching rules can supplement, not necessarily override, earlier ones — RainerScript's `stop` statement or explicit rule design controls this precisely).

p: Objective: Forward all logs to a central syslog collector over TCP.
Verification:
Objective: Set a custom rotation size/retention for a specific log file.
sections.code:
sudo tee /etc/rsyslog.d/99-forward.conf <<'EOF'
*.* @@central-collector.example.com:514
EOF
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog                              # 🟠

logger "test message from $(hostname)"     # 🟡 generates a test log entry
# on the collector: confirm the message arrived
ss -tnp | grep rsyslogd                    # 🟢 confirm an established outbound connection to the collector (TCP mode)

sudo vi /etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog     # 🟡 adjust size/rotate/compress directives for the relevant file stanza
sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog   # 🟠 force an immediate rotation to test the new config

list: Authentication/Authorization: modifying rsyslog config requires root.

Network exposure: plaintext syslog (UDP/TCP 514) sends log content, potentially including sensitive operational detail, unencrypted — prefer TLS-wrapped forwarding (6514) across untrusted network segments.
Firewall requirements: if operating as a remote collector, open only the specific inbound port needed, ideally restricted by source subnet via firewalld rich rules.
Sensitive files: `/var/log/secure` in particular contains authentication-relevant detail — protect with restrictive permissions (root-only readable is standard).

Logging/Auditing: rsyslog is itself part of the audit trail infrastructure — ensure its own availability/integrity is monitored, since a rsyslog outage silently stops flat-file/forwarded logging while journald (Profile 6) may continue locally.
Required security configuration: restrict log file permissions; avoid unauthenticated, unencrypted forwarding across untrusted networks for sensitive log content.
Optional hardening: TLS mutual authentication between forwarders and the central collector for high-assurance environments.

p: A common SELinux issue: configuring rsyslog to write to a nonstandard log path outside `/var/log/` without labeling it appropriately — fix with `semanage fcontext`/`restorecon` (Profile 5), not by disabling enforcement.
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep rsyslogd            # expect syslogd_t
ls -Z /var/log/                  # confirm expected var_log_t (or facility-specific) contexts
semanage port -l | grep syslog   # confirm port labeling if using a non-default forwarding port
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c rsyslogd

p: Common mistake: opening 514 inbound on every host in a fleet under the mistaken assumption it's needed for outbound forwarding — only the central collector needs an inbound allow rule.
sections.code:
firewall-cmd --add-port=514/tcp --permanent    # 🟡 only needed if operating as a COLLECTOR (inbound); a forwarding-only client needs no inbound rule
firewall-cmd --add-port=6514/tcp --permanent   # 🟡 TLS-wrapped collector port, if used
firewall-cmd --reload                          # 🟠

p: (rsyslog is a core logging component — this section covers its own operational self-diagnostics.)
sections.code:
journalctl -u rsyslog                       # 🟢 rsyslog's own daemon lifecycle/error events
tail -f /var/log/messages                   # 🟢 live view of general system messages
rsyslogd -N1                                # 🟢 validates configuration syntax without starting the daemon — run this before restarting after any config change

systemctl is-active rsyslog
rsyslogd -N1                       # config syntax check
logger "verification test $(date)"
grep "verification test" /var/log/messages     # confirm the local write path works
ss -tnp | grep rsyslogd            # confirm forwarding connection state if configured

list: Availability: validate config with `rsyslogd -N1` before every restart in production.
Security: prefer TLS-wrapped forwarding for cross-network log shipping; restrict collector-side inbound firewall rules by source.

Monitoring: monitor rsyslog's own health (`systemctl is-active`) and confirm forwarding connectivity as part of infrastructure monitoring — a silently-broken forwarding pipe can go unnoticed for a long time otherwise.
Configuration management: manage rsyslog config centrally for fleet-wide consistency, particularly the forwarding destination and any compliance-mandated facility routing.
Disaster recovery: ensure the central collector itself has redundancy/backup, since it may be the sole durable copy of logs from hosts that don't retain long local history.

p: Very high log volume (e.g., a misbehaving application logging excessively) is the most common source of rsyslog-related performance concern — address at the source (reduce log verbosity) rather than tuning rsyslog itself as a first response.
sections.code:
top / ps                     # 🟢 rsyslogd's own CPU/memory footprint, if suspected of overhead under very high log volume
iostat -x 1                  # 🟢 disk I/O if heavy local flat-file writing is a concern
ss -s                        # 🟢 connection state if forwarding over TCP and suspecting network-related backpressure

failures.fix: 🟡 Editing `/etc/rsyslog.conf`/drop-ins and restarting without first running `rsyslogd -N1` — a syntax error can prevent the daemon from starting at all, silently halting all flat-file and forwarded logging.
🟡 Confusing UDP (`@`) and TCP (`@@`) forwarding syntax, leading to unreliable delivery when reliable delivery was actually intended.
🟠 Opening inbound 514/6514 in firewalld on every host in a fleet rather than only the collector.
🟡 Forwarding sensitive log content in plaintext across untrusted network segments.

🟡 Assuming rsyslog and journald are redundant/interchangeable — they serve different purposes (structured local indexed queries vs. flat-file/network forwarding compatibility) and are commonly run together, with rsyslog frequently sourcing from journald via `imjournal`.
🟠 Not verifying `logrotate` is correctly configured for a custom log destination, leading to unbounded file growth.

trouble: Problem: Expected log entries aren't appearing in a file or at the remote collector.

Package:        rsyslog
systemd unit:   rsyslog.service
Daemon:         /usr/sbin/rsyslogd
Configuration:  /etc/rsyslog.conf, /etc/rsyslog.d/
Logs:           /var/log/messages, /var/log/secure, and other facility-specific files
Ports:          UDP/TCP 514 (traditional), TCP 6514 (TLS-wrapped, common convention)

Verification:

Critical warnings:
  🔴 Always run `rsyslogd -N1` before restarting after any config change.
  🟡 Prefer TLS-wrapped forwarding over plaintext syslog across untrusted networks.
  🟠 Only the collector needs an inbound firewalld rule — not forwarding clients.

title: Samba / SMB
analogy: Think of Samba as a translator standing between a RHEL filesystem and a room full of Windows machines that only speak "SMB" — Windows clients ask for files the way they normally would from a Windows file server, and Samba translates those requests into ordinary Linux filesystem operations, then translates the response back into SMB protocol terms.

sections.code:
Windows/SMB client
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Firewall (firewalld) — TCP 445 (modern SMB), historically also 139/137/138 for NetBIOS-based SMB1
   ↓
smbd (per-connection handling)
   ↓
smb.conf (share definitions, access control)
   ↓
winbindd (if domain-joined — maps AD identities to local UID/GID)
   ↓
Permissions / SELinux (samba_share_t and related contexts) + standard Unix permissions
   ↓
Underlying filesystem (Data)

rpm -q samba samba-client samba-common   # 🟢
sudo dnf install samba samba-client      # 🟡
smbd -V                                   # 🟢 version
testparm                                  # 🟢 validates smb.conf syntax and shows the effective (resolved) configuration

systemctl status smb
systemctl start smb
systemctl stop smb            # 🔴 clients immediately lose access to all shares
systemctl restart smb         # 🟠 drops all active SMB sessions
systemctl reload smb          # 🟡 re-reads smb.conf for most settings without dropping existing sessions — preferred for share/config changes; some changes still require restart (verify with testparm and documentation for the specific directive)
systemctl enable smb
systemctl is-active smb
systemctl status winbind      # if domain-joined

list: Main config: `/etc/samba/smb.conf`
Local user database (if not domain-joined): managed via `smbpasswd`/`pdbedit` (backend configurable, `tdbsam` is a common default for standalone servers).
Logs: `/var/log/samba/` (per-daemon and, depending on config, per-client log files), plus journald.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect

`[sharename]` block — Defines a share — `[public]`
`path = /srv/samba/public`
`browseable = yes`
`writable = no` — Creates a named share Windows clients can connect to
`valid users` / `write list` — Share-level access control — `valid users = @sambashare` — Restricts share access to members of a specific group
`security = user` (or `ads` for domain mode) — Authentication model — `security = ads` — `ads` mode integrates with an Active Directory domain rather than a local Samba user database

`map to guest` — Guest access behavior — `map to guest = Bad User` — Controls how failed/unknown-user authentication is handled — a security-relevant setting to configure deliberately, not leave at an unexamined default
Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
TCP — 445 — Modern SMB over TCP (SMB2/SMB3) — Primary port for current SMB versions; restrict to trusted networks

TCP/UDP — 137, 138, 139 — Legacy NetBIOS-based SMB (SMB1-era) — Should generally remain closed unless specifically required for legacy client support — SMB1 itself is deprecated/insecure and should be disabled in `smb.conf` where possible
sections.code: ss -lntup | grep smbd    # 🟢 confirm listening on 445

list: Service dependencies: `winbindd` if domain-joined; potentially SSSD-adjacent identity resolution depending on architecture chosen.
Network dependencies: firewalld allowing 445 (and legacy ports only if genuinely needed); DNS resolution consistent with any AD domain integration.
Storage dependencies: share paths must exist with correct ownership; sufficient space for the shared content.
Authentication dependencies: local Samba user database, or AD domain (via `security = ads` + `winbind`/`realmd` join) for centralized identity.
Security dependencies: SELinux `samba_share_t` labeling for shared directories; firewalld port restriction; `smb.conf` protocol version floor (disable SMB1).
Configuration dependencies: `testparm` syntax/semantic validation before every reload/restart.

p: Objective: Create a simple authenticated file share.
Verification:
Expected result: Windows/SMB clients can now connect to `\\SERVER\teamshare` and authenticate as `someuser`.
sections.code:
sudo mkdir -p /srv/samba/teamshare                                # 🟡
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t "/srv/samba/teamshare(/.*)?"   # 🟡 (Profile 5)
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/samba/teamshare                          # 🟡
sudo tee -a /etc/samba/smb.conf <<'EOF'
[teamshare]
    path = /srv/samba/teamshare
    valid users = @sambashare
    writable = yes
    browseable = yes
EOF
sudo testparm                                                      # 🟢 validate BEFORE reload
sudo systemctl reload smb                                          # 🟡
sudo smbpasswd -a someuser                                         # 🟡 set an SMB password for a local Samba user, if using local (non-AD) auth

smbclient -L localhost -U someuser    # 🟢 list shares, confirm the new one is visible
firewall-cmd --add-service=samba --permanent && firewall-cmd --reload   # 🟡🟠 if not already open

list: Authentication: local Samba user database or AD domain integration (`security = ads`); SMB passwords are separate from the underlying Linux account password unless synchronized deliberately.
Authorization: share-level (`valid users`, `write list`) plus standard Unix filesystem permissions — both apply.
Least privilege: scope shares narrowly (`valid users`) rather than broad guest access; disable guest/anonymous access unless specifically required.
Network exposure: restrict SMB (445) to trusted network segments via firewalld; never expose SMB directly to the open internet.
Protocol version: disable SMB1 (`server min protocol = SMB2` or later, verify current recommended minimum) — SMB1 has known, serious security weaknesses and is deprecated industry-wide.
Sensitive files: the local Samba password database (if used) and `smb.conf` (reveals share topology).
Required security configuration: SMB1 disabled; narrow `valid users` scoping; firewalld restricted to trusted networks.

Optional hardening: SMB signing/encryption requirements (`server signing = mandatory`, `smb encrypt = required` or similar current directives — verify exact current directive names/defaults against your Samba version's documentation).

sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep smbd
ls -Z /srv/samba/                       # expect samba_share_t
getsebool -a | grep samba
setsebool -P samba_export_all_rw on     # broad — prefer targeted fcontext labeling per share where feasible
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c smbd

p: Avoid opening the legacy NetBIOS ports (137-139) unless a specific legacy client genuinely requires them.
sections.code:
firewall-cmd --list-services | grep samba
firewall-cmd --add-service=samba --permanent    # covers the standard modern SMB port set in firewalld's service definition
firewall-cmd --reload                            # 🟠

journalctl -u smb                       # 🟢
tail -f /var/log/samba/log.smbd         # 🟢 per-daemon log
testparm -v                              # 🟢 verbose effective-configuration dump, useful when diagnosing "why isn't my directive taking effect"

systemctl is-active smb
testparm                       # confirms syntax and shows effective config
smbclient -L localhost -U USERNAME
ss -lntup | grep smbd
firewall-cmd --list-services

list: Security: disable SMB1; restrict network exposure; require SMB signing/encryption per current guidance.
Availability: prefer `reload` over `restart` for config changes where the specific directive supports it (verify via `testparm`/documentation).
Monitoring: monitor `smbd` health and, if domain-joined, the health of the domain trust relationship (`wbinfo -t`).
Configuration management: manage `smb.conf` and share definitions centrally for consistency across file servers.
Disaster recovery: back up `smb.conf` and, if using a local (non-AD) user database, the password backend as well.

sections.code:
smbstatus                # 🟢 shows current connections, locked files, share usage
top / ps aux | grep smbd  # 🟢 per-connection process resource usage
iostat -x 1               # 🟢 underlying storage I/O if file-serving performance is in question

lab.text: Confirm Samba installed; `testparm`.
Create a simple share with `valid users` restriction; apply SELinux labeling.
Set an SMB password for a lab user; connect with `smbclient`.
Verify firewalld allows the `samba` service.
(Lab VM only) Introduce a syntax error in `smb.conf`; observe `testparm`'s error output.
Fix and reload; verify with `smbclient -L` again.
(Optional, if lab infrastructure allows) Practice a basic AD domain join with `realm join` and observe `wbinfo -t`.

failures.fix: 🟡 Forgetting `testparm` before reload/restart — smb.conf syntax errors can prevent the daemon from applying (or even starting with) the intended configuration.
🟡 Forgetting SELinux `samba_share_t` labeling on a new share path — classic "access denied despite correct Unix permissions."
🟡 Confusing the Samba/SMB password with the underlying Linux account password — they're separate unless explicitly synchronized.
🟠 Leaving SMB1 enabled unnecessarily — a real, well-known security exposure.
🟡 Opening legacy NetBIOS ports (137-139) without a genuine legacy-client requirement.
🟡 Overly broad guest/anonymous access instead of scoped `valid users`.

trouble: Problem: A client can't connect to or authenticate against a share.

Package:        samba, samba-client, samba-winbind (if domain-joined)
systemd unit:   smb.service (+ winbind.service if domain-joined)
Daemon:         /usr/sbin/smbd (+ /usr/sbin/winbindd)
Configuration:  /etc/samba/smb.conf
Logs:           /var/log/samba/, journalctl -u smb
Ports:          TCP 445 (modern SMB); legacy 137-139 (avoid unless required)

Essential commands:
  testparm
  systemctl reload smb
  smbclient -L localhost -U USER

Verification:
  testparm && smbstatus && smbclient -L localhost

Troubleshooting:
  testparm → firewall-cmd --list-all → ls -Z → smbstatus → tail log.smbd

Critical warnings:
  🔴 Never expose SMB (445) directly to the open internet.
  🟡 Disable SMB1 — it is deprecated and insecure.
  🟡 Always `testparm` before reload/restart.

title: SELinux
analogy: Think of standard file permissions as a building's door locks (owner/group/other can open certain doors), and SELinux as an additional security guard standing at every door who checks a separate ID badge system ("types" and "contexts") regardless of whether the door lock would have let you through. Even if you have the right key (Unix permission), the guard (SELinux) can still refuse you if your badge (process type) doesn't match what that door (file/port/resource type) is cleared for.

p: SELinux and firewalld/DAC permissions are independent, all-must-agree gates — fixing one does not compensate for a denial in another.
sections.code:
Process (labeled with a domain type, e.g., httpd_t)
   ↓
Requested action (read file, bind port, connect socket, etc.)
   ↓
Kernel LSM hook → SELinux policy decision
   ↓
Policy: is there an "allow SOURCE_TYPE TARGET_TYPE:CLASS PERMISSION" rule?
   ↓
YES → action proceeds (still subject to normal DAC permissions too)
NO  → action denied, AVC logged (auditd/journald)
   ↓
Administrator: ausearch/sealert → identify → fix labeling or add policy exception

p: SELinux is part of the RHEL 10 base kernel and default install; it cannot be "installed" separately, but the policy/tooling packages can be verified:
sections.code:
rpm -q selinux-policy selinux-policy-targeted policycoreutils   # 🟢
sestatus                                                         # 🟢

p: There is no `systemctl start/stop selinux` — enforcement is a kernel-wide mode, not a service.

Persisting the mode requires editing `/etc/selinux/config` and generally a reboot (switching Disabled↔Enabled requires a reboot and a full filesystem relabel; switching Enforcing↔Permissive while already enabled does not require a reboot).

Why there's no "reload" concept: SELinux policy is loaded into kernel memory; changing the mode (enforcing/permissive) is instantaneous via `setenforce`, but changing the policy itself (adding a module, a boolean) uses `semodule`/`setsebool`, which load without a reboot.
sections.code:
getenforce                          # 🟢 Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled
sestatus                            # 🟢 detailed: policy type, mode, mount point
sudo setenforce 0                   # 🟠 switch to Permissive at RUNTIME ONLY (not persistent, logs denials but doesn't block them)
sudo setenforce 1                   # 🟡 switch back to Enforcing at runtime

list: Main config: `/etc/selinux/config` — sets `SELINUX=enforcing|permissive|disabled` and `SELINUXTYPE=targeted` (RHEL default policy).
Policy store: `/etc/selinux/targeted/` (compiled policy modules, contexts).
File context definitions: managed via `semanage fcontext` (persisted to `/etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts.local`).
Booleans: runtime-tunable policy switches, listed via `getsebool -a`, changed via `setsebool` (add `-P` for persistent).
Logs: AVC denials go to the audit log (`/var/log/audit/audit.log` — Profile 8) and are mirrored to journald.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`SELINUX=` — Overall mode — `SELINUX=enforcing` — Blocks and logs denied actions (vs. `permissive`: logs only, vs. `disabled`: no SELinux at all)
`SELINUXTYPE=` — Which policy set to load — `SELINUXTYPE=targeted` — RHEL default — confines specific network-facing daemons; `mls` is a stricter, rarely-used alternative

p: Not a network service itself, but SELinux labels ports to control which process types may bind them — directly relevant to every network-service profile in this handbook.
sections.code:
semanage port -l | less              # 🟢 list all port-to-type mappings
semanage port -l | grep http_port_t  # 🟢 e.g., which ports httpd_t may bind
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080   # 🟡 add a new port to an existing type

list: Service dependencies: kernel LSM framework; `auditd`/journald for denial logging (SELinux functions even without auditd running, but you lose visibility into denials).
Network dependencies: none directly.
Storage dependencies: filesystem must support extended attributes (xattrs) to store `security.selinux` labels — standard on RHEL's default filesystems.
Authentication dependencies: SELinux users (distinct from Linux users) map via `semanage login`, relevant mostly in MLS/high-security deployments, not typical targeted-policy servers.
Security dependencies: works alongside DAC permissions and firewalld — all three must independently permit an action.

Configuration dependencies: correct file/port labeling; a relabel (`restorecon`/`fixfiles`) is needed whenever files are created/moved in ways that bypass normal package-management labeling (e.g., manual `cp` from a tarball).

p: Objective: Diagnose and fix a denial (e.g., a web server can't read files in a nonstandard content directory).
Verification:
Expected result: the web server can now read the content without a denial, with SELinux still fully enforcing everywhere else.
Objective: Enable a boolean permitting a common cross-service behavior.
sections.code:
ausearch -m avc -ts recent                     # 🟢 find the denial
sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log            # 🟢 (if setroubleshoot installed) human-readable explanation + suggested fix
ls -Z /srv/mycustomsite                        # 🟢 see current context
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mycustomsite(/.*)?"   # 🟡 define the correct context persistently
restorecon -Rv /srv/mycustomsite               # 🟡 apply it

ls -Z /srv/mycustomsite       # 🟢 confirm httpd_sys_content_t now applied

getsebool httpd_can_network_connect            # 🟢 check current state
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on # 🟡 persistent change

list: Authentication/Authorization: changing SELinux mode/policy requires root.
Privilege requirements: `setenforce`, `semanage`, `setsebool -P` all require root.
Least privilege: this is the least-privilege mechanism for confined daemons — the "required security configuration" for this profile is simply: stay in Enforcing mode in production, always.

Never set `SELINUX=disabled` or run `setenforce 0` as a routine fix — this is explicitly the anti-pattern this entire handbook (and Red Hat's own guidance) warns against. Permissive mode has legitimate short-term diagnostic uses; Disabled removes the protection entirely and additionally requires a full relabel to safely re-enable later.
Sensitive files: the policy store itself (`/etc/selinux/targeted/`) should not be arbitrarily writable.
Optional hardening: move from `targeted` to `mls` policy only in environments with a specific mandate (government/high-assurance) — it is operationally heavier and not a default recommendation.

p: (SELinux is the subject of this profile — the full command set is used throughout; consolidated here.)

Contexts: `user:role:type:level` — administrators work almost entirely with type. File labeling: stored as an xattr; drifts when files are copied/moved outside package-manager-tracked operations — `restorecon` restores the policy-defined default. Booleans: pre-built on/off switches for common policy variations (e.g., "can httpd connect to the network") — always prefer an existing boolean over a custom policy module when one exists. AVC denials: the audit event type logged when policy blocks an action — `ausearch -m avc` is the first command to run whenever "permission denied"-shaped symptoms appear on an otherwise-correctly-permissioned resource. Troubleshooting SELinux denials: identify the denial (`ausearch`/`sealert`) → determine if it's a labeling problem (fix with `restorecon`/`semanage fcontext`) or a genuinely missing policy allowance (consider a boolean first, a custom module only as a last resort, reviewed line-by-line before loading) → verify → confirm no new denials appear for the same workflow. RHEL 10 note: `audit2allow`/policy tooling in RHEL 10 supports CIL (Common Intermediate Language) output, giving more transparency into exactly what a generated module grants — review the CIL output before loading any generated module rather than trusting the human-readable summary alone.
sections.code:
getenforce
sestatus
ls -Z /path/to/file
ps -Z
semanage fcontext -l | grep PATTERN
semanage port -l | grep TYPE
restorecon -Rv /path
getsebool -a
setsebool -P BOOLEAN on|off
ausearch -m avc -ts recent
audit2allow -w -a           # 🟢 human-readable "what would fix this" explanation
audit2allow -a -M mymodule  # 🟡 GENERATES a custom policy module — review before loading
semodule -i mymodule.pp     # 🟡 loads a custom policy module — do not do this blindly; audit2allow's suggestions can be overly broad

p: SELinux and firewalld are independent controls that both gate network-service reachability — see the port-labeling example in Section 7, and refer to each network-service profile's own Section 11/12 pairing for the specific interaction (e.g., Profile 4's SSH port-change walkthrough).

Always correlate an AVC denial's timestamp with the service's own log (`journalctl -u SERVICE`) — the denial and the user-visible symptom ("permission denied," a blank page, a failed bind) happen at the same moment and confirm causation.
sections.code:
journalctl -t setroubleshoot          # 🟢 if setroubleshoot is installed, human-friendly summaries land here too
ausearch -m avc -ts recent            # 🟢 primary tool — see Profile 8 (auditd) for the full audit-log toolkit
aureport --avc -i                     # 🟢 summarized, interpreted AVC report

p: "No new AVC denials during a full functional test of the service" is the actual verification goal — an absence of errors in the service's own log is not sufficient on its own, since SELinux denials sometimes manifest as generic errors in the application rather than SELinux-specific text.
sections.code:
getenforce                    # expect: Enforcing
sestatus                      # confirm policy=targeted, mode=enforcing, mode from config file=enforcing
ausearch -m avc -ts today     # expect: no unexpected recent denials for the workflow you just tested

list: Security: Enforcing mode is the required baseline for any production RHEL system; this is Red Hat's own stated position, not merely a hardening suggestion.
Monitoring: feed AVC denials into your SIEM/log aggregation (via auditd/rsyslog) — an unexpected new denial after a deployment is often the first signal of a config or code change gone wrong.
Configuration management: contexts (`semanage fcontext` additions) and booleans should be defined declaratively in configuration management, not applied ad hoc and undocumented.
Disaster recovery: back up custom fcontext/boolean/module state; after restoring files from backup, always `restorecon -Rv` before assuming they're correctly labeled.

p: SELinux's AVC (Access Vector Cache) caches policy decisions, so steady-state overhead is typically small (commonly cited as low single-digit percent on modern kernels) but is workload-dependent and not something to assume without measuring on your actual system:
If SELinux overhead is genuinely suspected as a bottleneck (rare), measure with `avcstat` before concluding it's the cause — don't assume and disable.
sections.code:
ps -eZ | head                # 🟢 sanity-check process contexts under investigation
top / vmstat                 # 🟢 general CPU check if suspecting SELinux overhead
avcstat                      # 🟢 (if installed) AVC cache hit/miss statistics

lab.text: Confirm current mode: `getenforce`, `sestatus`.
Create a lab directory and copy a file into it from `/tmp` (which has a different default context) — observe `ls -Z` shows an unexpected type.
Configure a service (e.g., httpd in a lab VM) to serve from that directory; observe a 403/permission error.
Use `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` to find the denial.
Fix with `semanage fcontext -a` + `restorecon -Rv`; re-test.
Practice toggling a boolean (`setsebool -P`) relevant to a lab service.
(Lab VM only) Run `setenforce 0`, reproduce the earlier failure now succeeding, confirming SELinux was the cause; then re-enable enforcement.
(Lab VM only) Practice `touch /.autorelabel` + reboot to observe a full relabel cycle.
Verify final state with `sestatus` and a clean `ausearch` for the tested workflow.

failures.fix: 🔴 Setting `SELINUX=disabled` permanently as a "fix" for an unresolved denial — removes an entire security layer instead of spending five minutes with `ausearch`/`restorecon`.
🟠 Leaving the system in `setenforce 0` (permissive) after using it only as a diagnostic step, and forgetting to re-enable enforcement.
🟡 Copying files with `cp`/tar-extracting into a service's content directory without `restorecon` afterward — classic cause of "it was fine yesterday, now the new files 403."
🟡 Loading an `audit2allow`-generated module without reviewing what it actually grants — these are frequently broader than necessary.
🟡 Confusing SELinux users/roles with Linux users — day-to-day server troubleshooting is almost entirely about types, not the user/role fields.

🟠 Forgetting that `Disabled → Enforcing` requires a full filesystem relabel (`touch /.autorelabel` + reboot, or equivalent) — simply flipping the config value without a relabel can cause a storm of denials on next boot as accumulated unlabeled files are encountered.

trouble: Problem: A service fails an operation that looks like a permissions problem but `ls -l` looks correct.

Never jump straight to `setenforce 0` as the "fix" — that's a diagnostic step at most (to confirm SELinux is indeed the cause), never a resolution. If permissive mode makes the symptom disappear, that confirms SELinux was the cause and tells you to go fix labeling/policy — not to leave it permissive.
quickRef:
Service:        SELinux (kernel Mandatory Access Control subsystem)
Package:        selinux-policy, selinux-policy-targeted, policycoreutils
systemd unit:   none (kernel-resident; optional restorecond.service helper)
Daemon:         none (kernel LSM)
Configuration:  /etc/selinux/config, semanage-managed contexts/booleans
Logs:           /var/log/audit/audit.log (via auditd), journalctl -t setroubleshoot
Ports:          N/A (labels other services' ports via semanage port)

Essential commands:
  getenforce / sestatus
  ausearch -m avc -ts recent
  restorecon -Rv PATH
  semanage fcontext -a -t TYPE "PATTERN"
  setsebool -P BOOLEAN on

Verification:
  getenforce (Enforcing) && ausearch -m avc -ts today shows nothing new for the tested workflow

Troubleshooting:
  ausearch -m avc → sealert -a → restorecon or setsebool → re-test

Critical warnings:
  🔴 Never leave SELINUX=disabled or setenforce 0 as a permanent "fix."
  🟡 Review any audit2allow-generated module before loading it — it can be broader than intended.
  🟠 Disabled → Enforcing requires a full relabel — plan a maintenance window.
