title: SSSD
analogy: Think of SSSD as a company's local reception desk that maintains its own address book cache — instead of every application on the machine calling the far-away corporate directory (AD/LDAP) directly every time it needs to check who a user is, they ask the local reception desk (SSSD), which either answers from its own recently-cached copy or looks it up remotely and caches the answer for next time — including still being able to answer basic questions if the connection to the corporate directory is temporarily down.

sections.code:
Application (login, su, sshd, etc.)
   ↓
PAM / NSS (standard Linux interfaces)
   ↓
SSSD responders (pam_responder, nss_responder, etc.)
   ↓
SSSD domain configuration (which backend, and how)
   ↓
   ├── Active Directory (via sssd-ad, often set up through `realm join`)
   ├── LDAP (via sssd-ldap)
   ├── IdM/FreeIPA (via sssd-ipa)
   └── Kerberos (via sssd-krb5, often alongside AD/IPA for ticket-based auth)
   ↓
Local SSSD cache (/var/lib/sss/db/) — enables offline lookups/auth within cache validity
   ↓
Result returned to the requesting application

rpm -q sssd realmd adcli                 # 🟢
sudo dnf install sssd realmd adcli oddjob-mkhomedir samba-common-tools   # 🟡 typical package set for an AD join

p: Applying config changes: most `sssd.conf` changes require a full restart rather than a lighter reload — verify with `systemctl cat sssd` and current documentation for your version, but plan for `systemctl restart sssd` (🟠) as the standard path after editing `sssd.conf`, and validate first (Section 9).
sections.code:
systemctl status sssd
systemctl start sssd
systemctl stop sssd            # 🔴 breaks centralized login/lookup immediately for any account relying on SSSD (local accounts still work)
systemctl restart sssd         # 🟠 brief interruption to identity lookups/new authentications during restart; existing sessions are typically unaffected
systemctl enable sssd
systemctl is-active sssd

list: Main config: `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` — must be `0600`, owned by root, or SSSD will refuse to start (a very common "why won't SSSD start after I edited the file" cause).
Kerberos client config (if applicable): `/etc/krb5.conf`
realmd config (if used): `/etc/realmd.conf`
Cache: `/var/lib/sss/db/` (binary cache database — not meant to be hand-edited).
Logs: `/var/log/sssd/` (per-domain and per-responder log files), plus journald.
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`[sssd]` → `domains = ` — Which configured domain(s) are active — `domains = example.com` — Determines which backend(s) SSSD actively queries
`[domain/example.com]` → `id_provider` — Identity backend type — `id_provider = ad` — Selects AD, ldap, ipa, proxy, etc.
`cache_credentials` — Whether to cache credentials for offline auth — `cache_credentials = True` — Allows login using cached credentials if the remote provider is unreachable

`access_provider` / `ad_gpo_access_control` — Access-control enforcement model — `ad_gpo_access_control = enforcing` (upstream default since a past SSSD release — verify your installed version's actual default) — Determines whether AD Group Policy-based logon rights are enforced by SSSD

p: SSSD itself doesn't listen on a network port (it's a client-side broker); it makes outbound connections to whatever backend is configured:
list: Protocol — Port — Purpose — Security considerations
TCP/UDP — 389 (LDAP) / 636 (LDAPS) — LDAP/AD directory queries — Prefer LDAPS (636) or STARTTLS over plaintext LDAP where possible
TCP/UDP — 88 — Kerberos authentication — Standard Kerberos port
TCP — 3268 / 3269 — Global Catalog (AD-specific, if used) — Relevant for multi-domain AD forests
sections.code: ss -tnp | grep sssd     # 🟢 shows current outbound connections to configured backends

list: Service dependencies: systemd; PAM/NSS configuration must correctly reference SSSD (`authselect` is the modern RHEL tool for managing this, rather than hand-editing PAM files directly).
Network dependencies: reachability to the configured identity provider(s); DNS resolution consistent with the domain (especially for AD, where SRV records drive site/domain-controller discovery).
Storage dependencies: `/var/lib/sss/db/` for the cache; `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` permissions.
Authentication dependencies: Kerberos time-sync sensitivity — SSSD/Kerberos authentication can fail if chronyd (Profile 7) has let the clock drift beyond the allowed skew.
Security dependencies: correct `sssd.conf` permissions (`0600`); SELinux `sssd_t` context.
Configuration dependencies: `authselect` profile correctly enabling SSSD for PAM/NSS; consistent DNS between the RHEL host and the identity provider's domain.

p: Objective: Join a RHEL host to an Active Directory domain.
Verification:
Expected result: domain users can look up and authenticate on this host per the domain's access policy.
Objective: Restrict login access to a specific AD group after joining.
sections.code:
sudo realm discover example.com                      # 🟢 confirms domain is reachable/discoverable and shows which client software realmd would use
sudo realm join example.com -U administrator          # 🟡 prompts for the domain admin's password; configures sssd.conf, krb5.conf, and PAM automatically

realm list                          # 🟢 confirms the join succeeded and shows configuration details
id someuser@example.com             # 🟢 confirms user lookup resolves via SSSD
getent passwd someuser@example.com  # 🟢 confirms NSS integration works end-to-end
su - someuser@example.com           # 🟡 confirms actual authentication works (will prompt for that user's password)

sudo realm permit -g "Domain-Admins"       # 🟡 (exact group-name syntax/case sensitivity depends on your AD setup — verify)
sudo realm deny --all                       # 🟡 combined with the above, denies everyone except the permitted group

list: Authentication: delegates to the configured backend (AD/LDAP/IPA/Kerberos) — SSSD itself doesn't invent a new trust model, but its caching means recently-authenticated credentials may still work briefly offline, a deliberate trade-off between availability and strict real-time revocation.
Authorization: `realm permit`/`deny`, or more granular `access_provider`/GPO-based controls for AD.
Privilege requirements: joining a domain (`realm join`) requires domain-admin-equivalent credentials at join time; SSSD itself runs as its own service account thereafter.
Least privilege: scope which domain groups may log in (`realm permit -g`) rather than allowing all domain users by default.
Sensitive files: `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` (`0600` mandatory — contains connection details and potentially bind credentials for LDAP-mode setups), the Kerberos keytab if used (`/etc/krb5.keytab`).

Required security configuration: correct file permissions on `sssd.conf`; LDAPS/STARTTLS rather than plaintext LDAP where the backend is LDAP-based; accurate time sync (chronyd, Profile 7) for Kerberos.
Optional hardening: stricter `cache_credentials`/offline-auth timeout policy for higher-security environments where offline login should be minimized.

p: SELinux denials directly involving SSSD are relatively uncommon in stock configurations; more often, SELinux issues arise in adjacent areas like NFS home directories for domain users (`use_nfs_home_dirs`, Profile 12) or `oddjob-mkhomedir` home directory creation.
sections.code:
getenforce
ps -Z | grep sssd
ls -Z /etc/sssd/sssd.conf         # confirm expected context
ausearch -m avc -ts recent -c sssd

p: SSSD is an outbound client, not an inbound service — no inbound firewalld rule is needed for SSSD itself. Ensure outbound connectivity to the identity provider's required ports (Section 7) isn't blocked by an upstream/network firewall (firewalld's default outbound posture is permissive, so this is rarely a local firewalld issue, but is worth confirming on the network path).

sections.code:
journalctl -u sssd                       # 🟢
tail -f /var/log/sssd/sssd.log           # 🟢 general daemon log
tail -f /var/log/sssd/sssd_example.com.log   # 🟢 per-domain backend log — often the most useful for backend-specific auth/lookup failures

systemctl is-active sssd
realm list                     # confirms domain join status
id someuser@example.com
getent passwd someuser@example.com
sssctl domain-status example.com   # 🟢 (if available in your version) detailed domain connectivity/health status

list: Availability: understand and deliberately tune cache/offline-auth timeouts for your environment's risk tolerance.
Reliability: monitor domain-join health (`realm list`, `sssctl domain-status`) proactively rather than discovering a broken trust only when users can't log in.
Security: keep `sssd.conf` permissions correct; use LDAPS/Kerberos rather than plaintext LDAP; ensure chronyd is healthy (Profile 7) as a prerequisite for reliable Kerberos-based auth.

Configuration management: manage `sssd.conf` and `authselect` profiles centrally for fleet consistency, being mindful of the strict file-permission requirement in any automation that writes this file.
Disaster recovery: document domain-join procedures so a host can be re-joined quickly if its trust relationship breaks irrecoverably.

p: Slow logins are very often not an SSSD defect but backend (AD/LDAP) latency or DNS resolution delay — correlate SSSD's own logs with actual network/backend response times before assuming SSSD itself needs tuning.
sections.code:
sssctl cache-expire -E     # 🟠 (if you need to force a full cache refresh for testing — understand this triggers fresh lookups for everything, which can be a load spike against the backend)
top / ps aux | grep sssd    # 🟢 SSSD's own resource footprint
tail /var/log/sssd/sssd_DOMAIN.log   # 🟢 look for repeated timeout/retry patterns indicating backend latency

lab.text: Confirm `sssd`, `realmd`, `adcli` installed.
`realm discover` a lab domain; review the reported client-software choice.
`realm join` the lab domain; verify with `realm list`.
Confirm `id`/`getent` resolve a domain user.
Restrict login with `realm permit -g`; verify a non-permitted domain user is denied login while a permitted one succeeds.
(Lab only) Deliberately break time sync (large clock offset) and observe Kerberos-based authentication failures; fix via chronyd and re-verify.
(Lab only) Set incorrect permissions on `sssd.conf`; attempt `systemctl restart sssd`; observe the failure and correct it.

failures.fix: 🔴 Leaving `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` with incorrect permissions after a manual edit — SSSD will refuse to start, a very common and non-obvious failure mode for administrators used to less strict permission requirements on other config files.
🟡 Not checking Kerberos-sensitive time sync (Profile 7) when authentication mysteriously starts failing fleet-wide.

🟡 Assuming a domain join is permanent/self-healing — DNS changes, domain controller decommissioning, or trust changes on the AD side can silently break SSSD's connectivity without any local RHEL-side config change.

🟡 Confusing Samba/winbind-based AD integration (Profile 13) with SSSD-based integration — the two solve overlapping but distinct problems, and mixing them without understanding the architecture can cause conflicting identity resolution.
🟡 Forgetting to scope login access (`realm permit`) after joining, defaulting to allowing the entire domain to log in when that wasn't intended.
🟠 Ignoring the per-domain log file location (`sssd_DOMAIN.log`) and only checking the generic `sssd.log`, missing backend-specific error detail.

title: systemd / systemctl
analogy: Think of systemd as an airport control tower rather than a single air-traffic controller shouting instructions one plane at a time (the old SysV model). The tower knows every plane's (service's) dependencies — which runway (mount point) must be clear, which other planes (services) must be airborne first — and it launches as many as safely possible in parallel rather than one after another.

p: Every other profile's "Technical Architecture" diagram in this handbook sits underneath this one — systemd is the common substrate.
sections.code:
Kernel boot
   ↓
initramfs (dracut)
   ↓
systemd (PID 1)
   ↓
default.target (usually graphical.target or multi-user.target)
   ↓
   ├── sysinit.target → local-fs, swap, udev, cryptsetup
   ├── basic.target → sockets, timers, paths
   ├── multi-user.target → network, sshd, firewalld, chronyd, auditd, etc.
   └── graphical.target → multi-user.target + display manager
   ↓
Individual .service / .socket / .mount / .timer / .path units
   ↓
cgroups v2 (resource accounting + process containment per unit)
   ↓
journald (structured logs for every unit)

p: systemd is part of the minimal RHEL 10 base install and cannot be meaningfully "installed" separately.

🟢 Both read-only. If `rpm -q systemd` returns "package systemd is not installed," the system is not a standard RHEL install (unusual — e.g., certain minimal containers intentionally exclude systemd; RHEL 10 containers built with `podman`/`buildah` commonly omit it deliberately, see Profile 18).
sections.code:
rpm -q systemd
systemctl --version

p: start vs enable: `start` = runtime only; `enable` = boot-time only. Production changes almost always need both (`systemctl enable --now SERVICE` does both atomically).
stop vs disable: same runtime/boot-time split in reverse.

restart vs reload: `restart` breaks existing connections (🟠 disruptive); `reload` is designed to be transparent to clients (🟡 lower risk) — but only if the specific daemon actually supports reload logic; check with `systemctl cat SERVICE` for a defined `ExecReload=`. If none exists, `reload` silently does nothing meaningful or systemd reports it unsupported.
status vs is-active: `status` is for humans (multi-line, includes logs); `is-active` is for scripts (single word, clean exit code — 0 if active).

daemon-reload: Required any time you edit a unit file (main file or drop-in) — it tells systemd to re-read unit files from disk. It does not restart any services; it only refreshes systemd's in-memory model of the unit's definition. Forgetting it is one of the most common administrator mistakes (see Section 16).
Identifying failed services:
Inspecting dependencies:
list: Command — What it does — When to use
`systemctl status SERVICE` — Shows current state, recent log lines, main PID, cgroup tree — First command for any investigation
`systemctl start SERVICE` — Starts the unit now, does not persist across reboot — Bringing a stopped service up immediately
`systemctl stop SERVICE` — Stops the unit now, does not change boot-time behavior — Taking a service down for maintenance
`systemctl restart SERVICE` — Full stop then start — drops all in-flight connections/state — Config changes that the daemon cannot reload live

`systemctl reload SERVICE` — Sends the unit's defined reload signal (often `SIGHUP`) to re-read config without dropping connections — Config changes the daemon supports reloading (e.g., httpd, sshd on some options)
`systemctl enable SERVICE` — Creates symlinks so the unit starts at next boot — does not start it now — Persisting desired state
`systemctl disable SERVICE` — Removes those symlinks — does not stop it now — Removing from boot without an outage right now
`systemctl is-active SERVICE` — Prints just `active`/`inactive`/`failed` — scriptable — Health checks, automation
`systemctl is-enabled SERVICE` — Prints just `enabled`/`disabled`/`static`/`masked` — Auditing boot configuration
`systemctl cat SERVICE` — Prints the effective unit file including drop-ins merged in — Understanding actual config before editing
sections.code:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload      # 🟡 after any unit file edit
sudo systemctl restart SERVICE    # 🟠 apply the new definition

systemctl --failed              # 🟢 lists every unit in "failed" state
systemctl list-units --state=failed

systemctl list-dependencies SERVICE      # 🟢 what this unit pulls in
systemctl list-dependencies --reverse SERVICE   # 🟢 what depends on this unit

list: Unit file search order (lowest to highest precedence): `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` (package-provided defaults) → `/etc/systemd/system/` (administrator overrides/custom units — this is what you edit) → runtime-only units in `/run/systemd/system/`.

Drop-in overrides: `/etc/systemd/system/SERVICE.service.d/override.conf` — the correct way to override part of a vendor unit without copying the whole file. Created interactively with `systemctl edit SERVICE`.

systemd's own configuration: `/etc/systemd/system.conf` (system manager defaults), `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`, `/etc/systemd/logind.conf`, `/etc/systemd/resolved.conf` — each governs a systemd component, not units in general.
Runtime data: `/run/systemd/` (volatile, cleared on reboot).
Persistent data: unit files themselves; journal logs (see Profile 6, systemd-journald).
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`Restart=` — Auto-restart policy on exit — `Restart=on-failure` — Restarts only on non-zero exit/crash, not clean stop
`After=` — Ordering only (not a dependency) — `After=network-online.target` — Delays start order but doesn't require the target to succeed
`Requires=` — Hard dependency — `Requires=postgresql.service` — If the required unit fails, this unit is stopped too
`WantedBy=` — Boot target this unit attaches to when enabled — `WantedBy=multi-user.target` — Determines what `enable` actually wires up

p: Not applicable to systemd itself (it is not a network service). Socket-activated units (`.socket` files) can bind ports on systemd's behalf before the real service starts — relevant to some services in later profiles (notably some legacy setups). Verify any socket unit with:
sections.code: systemctl list-sockets      # 🟢

list: Service dependencies: systemd has none above it — it is PID 1.
Network dependencies: none for systemd core; `network-online.target` is a synchronization point other units order themselves After=.
Storage dependencies: `local-fs.target`, `remote-fs.target` gate units needing mounted filesystems.
Authentication dependencies: none directly (PAM is invoked per-unit via `systemd-logind` for login sessions).
Security dependencies: cgroups v2 and (optionally) SELinux contexts are applied per-unit via `ExecStart=` context transitions.
Configuration dependencies: unit files depend on correct `.wants`/`.requires` symlinks, which `enable`/`disable` manage — manual symlink edits are error-prone; always use `systemctl enable/disable`.

p: Objective: Create a custom, persistent long-running service unit.
Verification:
Expected result: service starts now and on every future boot.
Objective: Safely apply a config change to an existing vendor service via drop-in (never edit files under `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` directly — they are overwritten on package updates).
sections.code:
sudo systemctl edit --full --force myapp.service   # 🟡 opens editor for a new unit
sudo systemctl daemon-reload                        # 🟡
sudo systemctl enable --now myapp.service           # 🟡 enable + start

systemctl status myapp.service        # 🟢 expect "active (running)"
systemctl is-enabled myapp.service    # 🟢 expect "enabled"

sudo systemctl edit sshd.service     # 🟡 creates /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service.d/override.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload         # 🟡
sudo systemctl restart sshd          # 🟠 disruptive for existing SSH sessions' future reconnects only, not current sessions

list: Authentication/Authorization: systemctl operations that change system state require root or Polkit-granted privilege (typically via `sudo`). Read-only queries (`status`, `is-active`) can be permitted to non-root users depending on Polkit policy.

Least privilege: Unit files support extensive sandboxing directives — `ProtectSystem=`, `ProtectHome=`, `NoNewPrivileges=`, `PrivateTmp=`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=`. Required security configuration is whatever your organization's hardening baseline mandates (e.g., CIS benchmark); optional hardening beyond that is per-service sandboxing directives, applied incrementally.

Sensitive files: unit files themselves — a writable-by-non-root unit file is a privilege escalation path (systemd will refuse to load units with insecure permissions in some configurations, and will log a warning).
Logging/Auditing: All service start/stop/failure events are journaled and can be correlated with `auditd` if unit-level auditing is configured.
Never disable systemd security sandboxing as a "quick fix" for an application error — diagnose why the sandbox is blocking the app first (see Troubleshooting).

p: systemd itself runs unconfined at the kernel/init level, but it launches every managed service with the SELinux context defined in that service's own policy (often via `type_transition` rules triggered by the executable's file context), not by systemd. Relevant commands when a systemd-launched service fails due to SELinux:

Do not disable SELinux to fix a systemd-launched service; find and fix (or `semanage`/`restorecon`) the mislabeled resource — see each individual service profile's SELinux section for service-specific contexts.
sections.code:
getenforce                       # 🟢 Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled
sestatus                         # 🟢 detailed status
ps -Z | grep SERVICE_PROCESS     # 🟢 confirm running context matches expected _t type
ausearch -m avc -ts recent       # 🟢 find recent denials tied to the unit's PID/context

p: Not applicable to systemd directly (systemd is not a network-facing daemon). See each network-service profile.

Correlate a failed unit with the broader system state: check `journalctl -u SERVICE` for the daemon's own error, then `journalctl -b` around the same timestamp for kernel/SELinux/storage messages that may be the true root cause, then `ausearch` for AVC denials in the same window.
sections.code:
journalctl -u SERVICE                       # 🟢 all logs for this unit, oldest first
journalctl -u SERVICE -b                    # 🟢 since last boot only
journalctl -u SERVICE --since "30 minutes ago"   # 🟢
journalctl -xe                              # 🟢 recent logs with explanations, useful right after a failure
journalctl -p err -b                        # 🟢 only error-level+ messages since boot

list: `systemctl is-active SERVICE` → `active` means the main process is running per systemd's tracking.
`systemctl is-enabled SERVICE` → `enabled` means it will start at next boot.
`systemctl status SERVICE` → look for `Active: active (running) since …` and absence of recent restarts (`Main PID` churn is a red flag).
`systemctl list-units --failed` → should return nothing unexpected.
`systemd-analyze verify SERVICE.service` → 🟢 lints a unit file for syntax/dependency problems before you rely on it.
`systemd-analyze blame` / `systemd-analyze critical-chain` → 🟢 boot performance and ordering diagnostics.
Availability: `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=` and (optionally) `StartLimitBurst=`/`StartLimitIntervalSec=` prevents both silent death and restart storms.
Monitoring: `systemctl --failed` should be part of any health-check/monitoring integration; journald can forward to rsyslog or a remote aggregator (Profile 10).
Configuration management: treat `/etc/systemd/system/*.d/override.conf` files as code — manage via your configuration-management tool, not ad hoc edits, in fleets.
Disaster recovery: unit files and drop-ins should be included in your configuration backup scope (Section 20).

p: Use `top`/`ps`/`free`/`vmstat` for the underlying OS resource picture once you've identified which unit is implicated via the systemd-specific tools above.
sections.code:
systemd-analyze                    # 🟢 total boot time breakdown
systemd-analyze blame              # 🟢 slowest-starting units
systemd-analyze critical-chain     # 🟢 the critical path that determined total boot time
systemctl status SERVICE           # 🟢 shows CPU/memory if accounting enabled
systemd-cgtop                      # 🟢 live resource usage per cgroup/unit

lab.text: Installation/prep: Confirm systemd version and default target (`systemctl get-default`).
Basic configuration: Create a trivial `myapp.service` unit running `sleep infinity`.
Service management: Practice start/stop/enable/disable/is-active/is-enabled on it.
Verification: Confirm boot persistence by simulating with `systemctl daemon-reload` + reboot in a lab VM.
Security: Add `NoNewPrivileges=true` and `ProtectSystem=strict` to the drop-in; observe behavior change.
Client/server testing: N/A directly for this unit (use a real network service profile).
Intentional failure (lab VM only): Point `ExecStart=` at a nonexistent binary; observe `systemctl status` and journal output.
Troubleshooting: Work the Section 15 chain against the induced failure.
Recovery: Fix the path, `daemon-reload`, `restart`, verify.

failures.fix: 🔴 Editing files directly under `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` — overwritten silently on next package update. Always use `/etc/systemd/system/` overrides via `systemctl edit`.
🟠 Forgetting `daemon-reload` after editing a unit file — the running config silently stays stale.
🟡 Using `restart` when `reload` would have avoided an outage, or assuming `reload` worked when the unit has no `ExecReload=` defined.
🟡 Assuming running = working — a process can be "active (running)" while its actual function (e.g., accepting connections) is broken; always verify functionally, not just via `systemctl status`.
🟡 Assuming listening = reachable — a service can be bound to a port locally while firewalld or SELinux blocks external reachability. Always test end-to-end, not just `ss -lntup` on the host itself.
🟠 Manually creating/deleting symlinks in `.wants/` directories instead of using `enable`/`disable` — creates drift systemd itself doesn't fully understand until the next `daemon-reload`.

trouble: Problem: A unit fails to start.
Do not jump to "just disable SELinux" or "just restart it repeatedly" — both mask the actual defect. Walk the chain above in order; each step rules out one layer.

Common scenario — "systemctl restart did nothing, it's still using the old config": Almost always means the unit file was edited but `daemon-reload` was skipped, so systemd restarted the process using its still-cached (old) definition of the unit. Or, the application's own config file was edited but the daemon doesn't reread it on `restart` in the way expected (rare) — verify with `systemctl cat` that the intended unit file is actually what's loaded.

title: systemd-journald
analogy: Think of journald as a black-box flight recorder for the whole system: every subsystem's messages are captured with a consistent, rich set of metadata (who said it, when, which boot, which unit) into one indexed store, rather than each application writing its own free-text file in its own format that you'd have to `grep` differently.

sections.code:
Kernel (kmsg) ──┐
Services (stdout/stderr via systemd, or native sd_journal API) ──┼──→ systemd-journald
Syslog-compatible senders (via /run/systemd/journal/syslog) ──┘
   ↓
Indexed binary journal files
   ↓
   ├── /run/log/journal/ (volatile — default if /var/log/journal/ doesn't exist)
   └── /var/log/journal/ (persistent — used if that directory exists, or Storage=persistent forces it)
   ↓
journalctl (local queries) ──and/or── forwarded to rsyslog / systemd-journal-remote (Profile 10, remote/long-term)

p: journald is part of the base `systemd` package and cannot be installed/removed independently.
sections.code:
rpm -q systemd                     # 🟢
journalctl --header                # 🟢 confirms journald is active and shows current storage details

p: journald is a core, always-on systemd component — administrators almost never `stop`/`disable` it. Configuration changes are applied via `systemctl restart systemd-journald` (🟠) after editing `journald.conf`/drop-ins, or (for storage-mode switches) via `journalctl --flush` after creating `/var/log/journal/` (see Section 9).
sections.code:
systemctl status systemd-journald
systemctl restart systemd-journald   # 🟠 brief gap possible in log capture during restart; rarely needed
systemctl is-active systemd-journald
systemctl cat systemd-journald

p: Verification note: sources describing RHEL's out-of-the-box default for `Storage=` (whether `/var/log/journal/` exists by default on a fresh RHEL 10 install, making persistence effectively the default in practice, versus the documented `auto` fallback to volatile storage) were not fully consistent at the time of writing. Check for yourself with `journalctl --header` or `ls -la /var/log/journal/` immediately after any fresh RHEL 10 install rather than assuming either way — this materially affects whether you lose logs across your very next reboot.
list: Main config: `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`
Drop-ins: `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf`
Storage location: `/run/log/journal/` (volatile) or `/var/log/journal/` (persistent)
Directive — Purpose — Example — Effect
`Storage=` — Where/whether to persist logs — `Storage=persistent` — Forces `/var/log/journal/`, creating it if missing, ensuring logs survive reboot
`SystemMaxUse=` — Cap on total disk space the journal may consume — `SystemMaxUse=2G` — Prevents unbounded log growth from filling `/var`
`SystemKeepFree=` — Minimum free space to always preserve on the journal's filesystem — `SystemKeepFree=4G` — Journald stops growing before the disk truly fills
`MaxRetentionSec=` — Maximum age before entries are eligible for rotation/removal — `MaxRetentionSec=1month` — Time-based retention policy independent of size
`ForwardToSyslog=` — Whether journald also forwards entries to a running syslog daemon — `ForwardToSyslog=yes` — Needed for rsyslog-based long-term/remote archiving (Profile 10)

p: journald itself has no network listener by default. `systemd-journal-remote`/`systemd-journal-gatewayd` (separate, optional packages) can expose journal data over HTTP(S) for centralized collection — not enabled by default; if you enable them, treat the port like any other network service profile (firewalld + SELinux port labeling required).

list: Service dependencies: systemd core; effectively no dependency on other daemons to function.
Network dependencies: none for local logging; relevant only if remote journal forwarding is configured.

Storage dependencies: the filesystem backing `/var/log/journal/` (if persistent) must have adequate free space — journald's own `SystemKeepFree=`/`SystemMaxUse=` settings manage this, but the underlying filesystem still needs monitoring.

Authentication dependencies: none for local reads by root; unprivileged users can read journal entries only if they're in the `systemd-journal` group or the entries are otherwise permitted (adm group historically, verify current RHEL 10 group model on your system).
Security dependencies: SELinux confines `syslogd_t`-adjacent contexts for related components; journal files themselves are root:systemd-journal owned.
Configuration dependencies: correct directory ownership/permissions (`systemd-tmpfiles --create` sets these correctly when creating `/var/log/journal/` manually).

p: Objective: Enable persistent (disk-backed) journal storage.
Verification:
Expected result: logs now survive reboot.
Objective: Cap journal disk usage to prevent `/var` exhaustion.
sections.code:
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal                              # 🟡
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal    # 🟡 sets correct ownership/permissions
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/00-storage.conf <<'EOF'
[Journal]
Storage=persistent
EOF
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald                     # 🟠
sudo journalctl --flush                                     # 🟡 forces the switch from volatile to persistent now

journalctl --header | grep -i "File path"     # 🟢 confirm path is under /var/log/journal/
ls -la /var/log/journal/                      # 🟢 confirm populated

sudo tee -a /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/00-storage.conf <<'EOF'
SystemMaxUse=2G
SystemKeepFree=4G
EOF
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald   # 🟠

list: Authentication/Authorization: reading journal entries as non-root requires group membership (typically `systemd-journal`) — do not broaden this casually, since logs can contain sensitive operational detail.
Least privilege: grant read access to log-aggregation service accounts via group membership rather than running them as root.

Sensitive files: journal files can inadvertently capture sensitive data if an application logs secrets to stdout/stderr — this is an application-level hygiene issue, not something journald itself filters.

Logging/Auditing: journald is itself part of the logging chain that feeds compliance/audit workflows; ensure `Storage=persistent` and adequate retention for any compliance requirement, and forward to a remote/immutable store (Profile 10) if tamper-resistance is required, since local journal files can be altered by anyone with root on the box.
Required security configuration: persistent storage with size/time retention limits appropriate to your compliance needs; restrict read access appropriately.
Optional hardening: forward-and-seal to a remote log server so a compromised host can't retroactively edit its own audit trail.

p: SELinux denials involving journald itself are rare in stock configurations; more commonly you'll see denials from other processes attempting to write to non-standard log locations that should instead go through journald/rsyslog's expected paths.

list: Availability/Reliability: always set explicit `SystemMaxUse=`/`SystemKeepFree=` in production to prevent disk exhaustion.
Monitoring: monitor `journalctl --disk-usage` trend, and monitor for journald's own error conditions (e.g., corrupted journal files reported at boot).

Logging strategy: decide deliberately whether journald's persistent local storage is sufficient or whether forwarding to rsyslog/remote aggregation (Profile 10) is required for retention/compliance/tamper-resistance.

Backup: journal files themselves are not typically "backed up" in the traditional sense (they're operational logs, not primary data), but retention policy should match your compliance/incident-response requirements.
Disaster recovery: N/A directly — the concern is retention/availability of logs about other systems' disaster recovery, not journald's own DR.

p: High-volume logging services (e.g., a very chatty application logging at debug level in production) can generate meaningful I/O load through journald — the fix is almost always reducing the source's log verbosity, not tuning journald itself.

failures.fix: 🟡 Assuming logs persist across reboot without verifying `Storage=` and the existence of `/var/log/journal/`.
🟠 Setting no `SystemMaxUse=`/`SystemKeepFree=` limits on a long-running production server and being surprised when `/var` fills up.
🟡 Forgetting `journalctl --flush` after switching from volatile to persistent storage mid-uptime — the switch otherwise only fully takes effect from the next boot.
🟡 Broadening journal read access to too many users/groups, exposing operationally sensitive log content.

🟠 Relying solely on local journal storage for compliance/forensic purposes when an attacker with root could alter or vacuum it — forward to a remote target (Profile 10) for anything requiring tamper-resistance.
